notes.title: Who controls the movement
notes.body: 步步 doubles “step” so that each movement adds pressure. Its clipped four-character shape faces the bodily loss of control in the next line. Repeating this pair makes intimidation mechanical: one person controls the pace, the other cannot control even their own body. The later demand to kneel completes that unequal choreography.

notes.title: Fear arrives before the laugh
notes.body: 还没…呢 emphasizes that an expected action has not even happened yet. The opponent is already crying before the speaker begins to laugh, so the taunt presents fear as premature and excessive. It is a small contest over timing: the threatening figure claims not only greater strength, but the power to decide when the scene has truly started.

notes.title: A threat denies its own effect
notes.body: He has spent the opening applying pressure, then tells the frightened person that they are imagining persecution. The contradiction is the cruelty of the taunt: he controls both the threat and the account of whether it happened. Immediately afterwards, a cold and aching ears shrink the frightening figure to someone who wants quiet because he feels ill. These changes of scale keep the persona unstable. The psychiatric phrase is an insult in that performance, not a reliable diagnosis.

notes.title: A feature priced in bitcoin
notes.body: One bitcoin makes the feature sound inaccessible, but the later admission that he still lacks money undercuts a straightforward rich-rapper boast. A price can perform status before it produces income. The line is therefore also a way to refuse an inferior negotiation: he sets the terms so high that the other person cannot enter. The exact exchange rate is unnecessary to the joke, and the lyric is not a verified booking quote.

phrase.pinyin: yí gè feat yào yí gè bǐ tè bì

notes.pinyinLabel: yí gè feat yào yí gè bǐ tè bì

notes.title: Making the rival smaller
notes.body: 弟 already places someone below an older brother; 娃 adds the diminutive sense of a child. The regionally flavored address makes the feature-price boast sound like an older figure brushing off an inexperienced youngster. The insult is about rank as much as money: the other person is too small to negotiate on equal terms.

notes.title: No role left for you
notes.body: 没有戏 literally says there is no play or performance; colloquially it means something has no prospect of working out. Here it dismisses the other person’s chances immediately after pricing a feature. It need not mean that a literal stage role has been refused.

notes.title: A specific name behind “caveman”
notes.body: 山顶洞人 is the Chinese name for the prehistoric humans associated with the Upper Cave at Zhoukoudian, near Beijing. In this taunt, that recognizable name is compressed into “caveman,” then coupled with ritual dancing. The historical term supplies the image; the verse is not describing an archaeological practice.

sources.label: Chinese Academy of Sciences: Zhoukoudian Upper Cave research

notes.title: 套路 means a routine—and a ploy
notes.body: 套路 can mean an organized set of moves and, colloquially, a predictable maneuver or manipulative ploy. After the wriggling, silk-spitting spectacle fails to affect him, the speaker asks for simpler 套路. The word makes the display sound rehearsed rather than powerful.

notes.title: A limit inside the excess
notes.body: After dismissing other people's elaborate routines as ineffective, he distinguishes his own fixed boundary from their tricks. This is a claim to continuity—he says he has not changed—inside a verse that keeps changing tone. The distinction he asks us to accept is between theatrical behaviour and personal standards. Whether that self-description is entirely convincing remains part of the performance; the opening manipulation has already made his authority uncomfortable.

notes.title: A sudden turn to the dinner table
notes.body: 三鲜 means “three delicacies.” 地三鲜 is the familiar combination of eggplant, potato, and green pepper; 素三鲜 means a vegetarian trio, with the exact ingredients left unspecified here. After intimidation and the bitcoin feature price, the choice is suddenly an ordinary meal, followed by turning the serving tray and letting others eat first.

notes.pinyinLabel: sù sān xiān hái shì dì sān xiān

notes.title: The god observes table manners

phrase.en: Go ahead and dig in first
phrase.pinyin: kuài zi nǐ men xiān dòng

notes.body: Chinese table conversation can refer to beginning a meal as “moving the chopsticks.” After commanding somebody to kneel, the same voice now yields the first move to others at a shared table. The rotating serving tray, indecision over vegetables and small courtesy abruptly bring the self-styled god down to an ordinary communal meal.
notes.pinyinLabel: kuài zi nǐ men xiān dòng

notes.title: A familiar song phrase enters the chant

phrase.en: The light of the righteous path

notes.body: 正道的光 is recognizable from Huang Bo’s song 正义之道, documented in CCTV’s performance archive. Here its vocabulary of righteousness joins the black-and-white taiji image and the repeated “Lord Kai.” A phrase associated with moral uplift becomes part of an exaggerated personal coronation after the verse’s intimidation, bodily comedy and ordinary meal.

sources.label: CCTV: Huang Bo performs 正义之道

notes.title: The black-and-white diagram

phrase.pinyin: yī hēi yī bái tài jí

notes.body: 太极 is not limited to the martial art called tai chi in English. The explicit black and white also evoke the taiji diagram, a circle of interlocking yin and yang halves. That gives the line a compact visual emblem rather than necessarily describing someone doing exercises.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 太極圖

notes.pinyinLabel: yī hēi yī bái tài jí

notes.title: Kai becomes a title
notes.body: The title turns his given name into a godlike accolade. But the coronation follows a person unable to choose between vegetable dishes, spinning the serving tray and politely letting others eat first. That immediate context keeps the chant from becoming a purely solemn assertion of greatness. He can demand worship in one register and be a recognisably ordinary dinner companion in another. The comedy depends on allowing both pictures to remain.

tracks.intro: Kai keeps inflating and puncturing its own authority. The voice terrifies someone, calls their fear unreasonable, sets an extravagant price for a guest verse, then admits to limited money and gets distracted by vegetables. Its claim to have personal limits sits inside a performance that enjoys excess. The final self-coronation works because the ordinary man at the table remains audible inside the godlike persona. The shifts are part of the joke, rather than obstacles to finding one consistent, solemn message.

notes.title: Money as an exit
notes.body: 就 makes the sequence immediate: once the money is in hand, leave. The hook never stays to enjoy what has been acquired. Repetition makes cash feel less like a destination than permission to escape, a pattern sharpened by the later account of having to fight for a living.

notes.title: Trading up, with weapons as the image
notes.body: 鸟枪换炮 swaps a modest hunting gun for a cannon, an idiom for a dramatic improvement in means or circumstances. The scale of that upgrade contrasts with the later need to scrape together a meal. In between, the “secret” cannot be shared: the song puts the visible result of advancement next to the hidden means of obtaining it.

phrase.en: trading a musket for a cannon

notes.title: An identity worn by a car
notes.body: 套 here concerns using another vehicle’s registration identity, hence the translation’s “cloned” plates. Naming Hong Kong and Macau makes the image geographically specific; the vehicle wears credentials that do not straightforwardly belong to it. Coming after the secret of upgrading, that borrowed exterior prepares the later attack on an ugly 嘴脸, the face someone puts on.

sources.label: Shandong court: explanation of 套牌 in a plate-sharing case

notes.title: The same two characters, reversed
notes.body: Reversing the same two syllables changes a missed opportunity into wrongdoing. It follows questions about good and evil and precedes someone who can say both the flattering and the nasty thing as circumstances require. That sequence asks what happens when getting ahead becomes the measure of being right. It does not simply announce that morality is meaningless; it exposes how conveniently an account of necessity can be rearranged to justify a choice.

notes.title: Owning both sides of the argument
notes.original: 好话赖话都被你说完了

phrase.zh: 好话赖话都被你说完了
phrase.en: You've said every nice thing and every nasty thing
phrase.pinyin: hǎo huà lài huà dōu bèi nǐ shuō wán le

notes.body: 好话 and 赖话 place favorable and unfavorable speech in the same person’s mouth. 说完了 suggests they have used up both sides, leaving no position they have not already occupied. The accusation is not simply dishonesty; it is opportunistic flexibility, immediately reduced to the need to secure a bite to eat.
notes.pinyinLabel: hǎo huà lài huà dōu bèi nǐ shuō wán le

notes.title: A meal stands for a livelihood
notes.body: 讨口饭 or 讨口饭吃 can mean scraping out a living. The small mouthful makes basic subsistence the scale of the effort. Beside the insistence on getting money and running, it keeps the cash imagery tied to survival as well as ambition.

notes.title: Who gets to frame the struggle

phrase.en: what it looks like to fight to survive
phrase.pinyin: pīn mìng shēng huó de mú yàng

notes.body: Somebody else's camera turns the effort of staying alive into an image. Later, the hawker calls tell passersby not to miss a person on the verge of catastrophe. Together these moments make spectatorship part of the grievance: an exhausted person's life becomes interesting material for someone who can stand back from it. The song does not identify a specific photographer or platform. Its sharper claim is about the unequal positions of living the crisis and consuming its appearance.
notes.pinyinLabel: pīn mìng shēng huó de mú yàng

notes.title: A weather forecast for a face
notes.body: 局部多云 is “partly cloudy,” the phrasing of a weather report. Applying it to 脸色, facial appearance or expression, turns a bad mood into a forecast.

notes.title: Exhaustion before judgment

phrase.en: Of course you get lazy when you're too exhausted
phrase.pinyin: tài lèi le zì rán huì biàn lǎn

notes.body: This sentence reverses a familiar accusation. Inactivity is the result of depletion, not proof that a person never tried. It is especially pointed after the description of fighting to live being photographed: an observer can see the visible failure while missing the effort that produced it. The plain causal statement briefly cuts through the cash boasts and theatrical insults, giving the grey mood a practical explanation rooted in the body's limits.
notes.pinyinLabel: tài lèi le zì rán huì biàn lǎn

notes.title: The sound of a clearance sale
notes.body: The clearance-sale voice repeatedly interrupts private distress. Later, 'don't miss out' directly introduces someone about to cause a catastrophe, so the sales language acquires an object: the spectacle of another person's collapse. The song itself performs this attention-grabbing patter, which makes the position uncomfortable. It is criticising the appetite for a show through language that also knows how to gather a crowd.

notes.title: The bait meets somebody who will not bite
notes.body: 老奸巨猾 describes someone deeply practiced in deceit or cunning. There is no fox in the Chinese; English supplies its own familiar animal for that character. With a loach held at the mouth in the previous line, 不会咬 works both as refusing food and refusing to be lured in.

notes.title: The body stores what cannot be said

phrase.en: Pain with no outlet turns into fat

notes.body: 苦 is hardship, suffering, and bitterness; 脂肪 gives it a bodily storage place. The image makes blocked expression accumulate as matter. It belongs with the cloudy face and flashing body in the surrounding verse: what cannot be released in words returns as a surface or signal that others can see.

notes.title: A body told to stop and go
notes.body: The body becomes a traffic signal while it is barely managing to stay upright. Red and green offer incompatible instructions—stop and go—so the image fits a person required to continue while showing signs of strain. The next hawker call urges people not to miss the spectacle, making private warning signs into public attraction.

notes.title: A hard mouth and an uneasy heart
notes.body: 嘴硬 is refusing to concede or continuing to talk tough despite contrary evidence. The next line’s 心虚 is inward unease, guilt, or lack of confidence. Together they split the person into a defiant mouth and an insecure interior; the praise of how “cool” and “beautiful” this looks carries a mocking edge.

notes.title: Grey is also something that covers you
notes.body: The final grey is dust or ash covering a body. It follows sarcastic praise for looking cool while talking tough and beautiful while inwardly uneasy. That coating makes it hard to maintain the clean division between the confident exterior and what it conceals. It also brings the opening good-or-evil questions down to a worn, dirty surface. The last command to run restores the escape impulse; the song has not found a pristine place outside the mess.

tracks.intro: Grey puts the need to earn beside the ugliness of watching and selling other people's struggle. The opening cash-and-escape fantasy gives way to fatigue, a photographed body and street-market calls inviting spectators to watch a breakdown. Judgement keeps changing direction: the speaker condemns opportunism while also explaining how exhaustion deforms behaviour. The grey at the end is something that coats a person, not merely an abstract moral category. The song makes it difficult to keep survival, performance and complicity neatly apart.

notes.title: Reading the heat on a face
notes.body: The song opens with bodily discomfort before offering social advice. Later it tells the listener not to cry when the heat makes them sweat, blurring two kinds of moisture on a face. That small confusion prepares a track where expressions are unreliable and it is difficult to tell what people genuinely feel.

notes.title: A warning makes its own defense

phrase.en: If you hear it and don't remember

notes.body: The warning makes the listener responsible for remembering what they have been told, with an insult ready if they fail. That is the tough voice of someone claiming worldly experience. Later, however, the speaker admits that seeing another person's pain does not enable him to help. The song moves from sounding as though correct advice can prevent disaster to recognising the limits of advice. Its return to the warning does not erase that admission.

notes.title: Art is answered with a lack of skill
notes.body: 艺术, yìshù, ends with the same shù that closes 不学无术, bùxué-wúshù: having neither learning nor skill. The reply seizes the last sound of “art” and returns it as an accusation of incompetence. English carries the contempt but loses this quick verbal catch, where the lofty claim supplies the material for its own dismissal.

notes.title: Clarity becomes a costume
notes.body: 清白 means innocent or untainted, literally clear and white. It follows 清醒, being clearheaded, and precedes the accusation of pretending to be innocent. The shared 清, qīng, sound briefly builds an image of clarity before the next lines expose it as an act. The sequence lets pristine language do the work of camouflage.

notes.title: Indistinguishable faces become matching tiles
notes.body: 连连看 is a tile-matching game: identify repeated pictures and pair them away. It arrives immediately after “they all look the same,” making the surrounding people seem as interchangeable as game pieces. The narrator’s small private pastime becomes a way to judge a scene full of supposedly distinctive personalities.

sources.label: Developer description: 連連看 on Google Play

notes.title: Inspecting the scene as merchandise

phrase.pinyin: xiāo fèi zhě guān chá bào gào

notes.body: Inspecting people like merchandise creates distance: the observer can identify bad surfaces and faulty contents without entering a relationship with them. That stance fits the matching-game image, where supposedly individual people become interchangeable pieces. The later address to a particular beloved nuisance breaks this detached inspection. It is much easier to write off a social type than to watch someone you care about become trapped in the same world.
notes.pinyinLabel: xiāo fèi zhě guān chá bào gào

notes.title: The body beneath the respectable face

phrase.en: Organs with nowhere to run wild
phrase.pinyin: méi chù sā yě de qì guān

notes.body: 撒野 is behaving wildly or acting out without restraint. Giving that impulse to organs strips away the people’s respectable faces and leaves frustrated bodily drives. The line follows malice stored up for half a lifetime, so the behavior appears as pressure seeking an outlet rather than as an impressive form of freedom.
notes.pinyinLabel: méi chù sā yě de qì guān

notes.title: Why keep “jianghu” in English?
notes.body: 江湖, jiānghú, literally means rivers and lakes, but also names the wider social world a person has to navigate. It carries the sense of informal rules, experience and entanglement captured in the saying about not being free to act as one pleases within it. Here that world becomes a poison: belonging has entered people’s bodies and altered them.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 江湖

notes.title: A fragment left unresolved
notes.body: 水帘洞, Water Curtain Cave, is the hidden home reached through a waterfall in the first chapter of Journey to the West. Entering it establishes the stone monkey’s authority among the other monkeys. The name brings that childhood-familiar fantastic space into a verse of smoke and half-sleep; it offers a refuge-like image just after the claim that the social world has poisoned people.

sources.label: Journey to the West, chapter 1 (Shidetang edition)

notes.title: Change without improvement
notes.body: This familiar announcement often promises modernization or progress. The next two lines make its conclusion simply that things are worse. The deadpan turn refuses to let novelty count as improvement, just as the song refuses to let a polished look count as inner worth. The speaker’s test is what the change does to people.

notes.title: A polished exterior and rotten stuffing
notes.body: This phrase comes from Liu Ji’s parable of an orange seller: beautiful fruit contains pulp as dry as worn cotton wadding, and the seller compares it to impressive-looking officials who fail the people. Its everyday meaning is an attractive exterior hiding poor substance. Here it caps a catalog of innocent faces and respectable appearances, giving the judgment a long satirical ancestry.

sources.label: Ministry of Education idiom dictionary: 金玉其外，敗絮其中

phrase.en: Gold and jade outside, rotten stuffing within
phrase.pinyin: jīn yù qí wài bài xù qí zhōng

notes.pinyinLabel: jīn yù qí wài bài xù qí zhōng

notes.title: An exasperated form of address
notes.body: The affectionate, exasperated address changes the emotional scale. After condemning a whole crowd, he speaks to someone whose stumbling he has watched closely. 'Little ancestor' treats a demanding person as both troublesome and precious. The subsequent inability to rescue them therefore hurts: this is not simply an enemy receiving deserved punishment. The lyric lets concern interrupt its sweeping contempt without pretending the concern can fix anything.

notes.title: The social world has no clear exit
notes.body: Unlike an open road, a maze offers movement without a clear way out. One careless entrance traps the person; seeing their stumbling from outside does not give the narrator a route to rescue them. This is the song’s most sympathetic image of jianghu: a social world can ruin someone without that person fully understanding its layout.

notes.title: Wanting to help is not being able to

phrase.en: there's nothing I can do to help

notes.body: The segmentation is 可 / 爱莫能助: “but / willing to help yet unable to.” 可爱 is not “cute” here. The idiom preserves the speaker’s concern even as it admits powerlessness, which makes the following physical and emotional withdrawal more conflicted than a simple refusal to care.

notes.title: Three kinds of distance
notes.body: Physical, biological and emotional separation sound like successive stages of a technical procedure. Yet the need for a procedure exposes the difficulty of leaving: he has just said that he sees the other person's pain and cannot help. The final stage is not merely moving away but loosening an attachment. The imagery answers the earlier poison metaphor—contact has become damaging—while preserving the cost of protecting oneself from someone one still cares about.

notes.title: 骚 is wider than its literal sexual sense
notes.body: 骚, sāo, can describe sexual boldness, but colloquial praise also uses it for conspicuous flair or an outrageous move. “Flashy” captures that showy excess. After the long withdrawal into emotional isolation, the short exclamations suddenly sound like a spectator reacting to somebody’s display, with admiration and mockery still entangled.

tracks.intro: Jianghu begins as abrasive advice about surviving the social world, then discovers someone the speaker cannot simply dismiss. Its crowd of interchangeable, rotten people gives way to a troublesome 'little ancestor' whose pain he sees and cannot repair. Withdrawal becomes a procedure because affection alone does not make rescue possible. The opening warning returns, but now its harshness sits beside helpless care. The song is about what this world does to relationships, as much as about exposing the falseness of a scene.

notes.title: A prediction presented as fact
notes.body: Calling the opening a “fact” asserts authority before presenting any evidence. The following future-tense pursuit cannot yet be observed, but the phrase asks us to receive it as settled. That certainty shapes the entire chant: escape, luck and disbelief are all ruled out by a voice speaking as if the outcome has already happened.

notes.title: Vanity becomes the target
notes.body: The target is the desire to be admired. The following dream is therefore a form of capture, not a simple reward: the pursuer can keep someone inside an appealing account of themselves. No particular manager, rival or institution is identified. The mechanism is more general and more intimate than that: a person can be controlled through the story they most want to believe about their own importance.

phrase.pinyin: jū jī nǐ de xū róng xīn

notes.pinyinLabel: jū jī nǐ de xū róng xīn

notes.title: Luck and effort are set against each other
notes.body: 侥幸 especially suggests obtaining a good outcome or escaping trouble by chance. The following “no escape” makes that shade stronger than generic good fortune. Later, the speaker says he has kept working and fighting; the song grants others no lucky exit while claiming his own position through effort.

notes.title: A cheerful confectionery name over a threat

phrase.pinyin: mián huā táng pào pào táng

notes.body: HARIBO’s name brings the world of gummy sweets and colorful packaging into the title. The verse then names cotton candy and bubble gum before dismantling the sweetness into flavoring and color. The point is less a particular product than the distance between an inviting surface and what has been manufactured to produce it.
notes.pinyinLabel: mián huā táng pào pào táng

notes.title: Sweetness listed as ingredients
notes.body: Breaking sweets into flavouring and colouring removes the enchantment from an attractive whole. In the preceding lines, vanity makes a dream persuasive; here the lyric shows how an effect can be assembled. The title need not point to a particular HARIBO product for this to work. Sweetness becomes a model for validation that feels good to receive while telling you little about the substance behind it.

notes.title: 命 as fate
notes.body: The other person's future is treated as fixed, while the speaker later describes his own standing through continued effort. That unequal distribution of agency gives the warning an aggressive edge. He does not merely explain the trap; he speaks as though he is entitled to pronounce its victim's fate. The phrase 'believe it or not' allows disagreement only after the outcome has supposedly been decided.

notes.title: A choice that changes nothing
notes.body: The formula literally leaves belief up to you, but gives no choice over the outcome itself. Its apparent freedom is narrow: the listener can disagree internally while the predicted fate proceeds. That makes it a fitting answer to the title’s inviting candy image—acceptance can be offered without changing the trap.

notes.title: Effort keeps moving
notes.body: Hard work is offered as the substance missing from the manufactured dream. Yet the claim ends in a repeated 'I am number one', explicitly addressed to people who do not believe him. His own investment in recognition has not disappeared. The contrast can be heard as earned confidence, but the song also leaves him close to the vanity it has just attacked. Preserving that friction gives the boast more interest than treating it as automatic proof of authenticity.

tracks.intro: Haribo imagines vanity as a point of entry for manipulation: somebody offers a dream whose sweetness is manufactured. The speaker insists that the trap is inescapable, then switches to his own hard work and the claim to be number one. That juxtaposition leaves a productive discomfort. He wants to distinguish earned standing from flattering illusion, but his repeated need to assert first place also belongs to the world of recognition the song has made suspect. The unnamed pursuer remains unnamed; the lyric supplies a mechanism, not a confirmed personal exposé.

notes.title: An ordinary start leaves room for care
notes.body: The opening uses a few unadorned pieces of routine: afternoon, waking up, a call, a message. The confidence that every problem can be settled is built on those small actions. That ordinary scale makes the later direct plea to survive more intimate; the song begins close enough to daily life for care to arrive without a grand introduction.

notes.title: Invulnerability in four characters
notes.body: The opening promises to sort out every problem and remain immune to poison. Addressed through a call or message, that confidence can also do reassuring work for somebody else. It need not be a transparent report of an invulnerable inner state. The later stifling boredom and desire to disappear expose the limits of the claim. The voice can offer steadiness to a friend while struggling to remain comfortable in the wider scene.

notes.title: Calm as a surface of water
notes.body: 波澜 are waves or ripples, here transferred to the inner life. The speaker describes stillness immediately after firm will and immunity to poison, creating a picture of total composure. Later boredom becomes stifling and other people cannot stop. The image of calm is something the song has to preserve against a much noisier social environment.

notes.title: Not knowing the world can preserve something
notes.body: 见世面 means acquiring social experience and seeing how the wider world works. The next line gives the resulting naivety the unexpectedly approving description “pure.” Later, the speaker sees the social scene clearly enough to want to become invisible, complicating the idea that more exposure is always better.

notes.title: A blessing measured by appetite
notes.body: 福气 is the good fortune of a life going well. Its measure here is simply being able to eat and drink. That bodily minimum sits far below the money, fashion and rank flaunted elsewhere on the mixtape. The instruction to keep living grows out of this modest definition of a good life, rather than out of a demand to achieve more.

notes.title: What the request actually asks

phrase.pinyin: hǎo hǎo de huó xià qù

notes.body: He asks the friend to keep living for the friend's own sake. That matters beside a record full of money, usefulness and other people's demands: continued existence does not have to be justified by producing something for an audience. The everyday blessing of eating and drinking prepares this modest standard. When these lines return at the end, after repeated 'whatever', they establish what his withdrawal is meant to leave room for.
notes.pinyinLabel: hǎo hǎo de huó xià qù

notes.title: An address to a longstanding companion
notes.body: 老 can mark familiarity or longstanding closeness rather than advanced age; 兄弟 often addresses a male friend or companion. The repeated address makes the plea to keep living feel personally directed. It need not identify a biological sibling.

notes.title: The substance is not named
notes.body: The speaker says 'I guess', then declines to hear details. Ear studs and gold teeth become grounds for a judgement he does not verify. Keeping that wording visible prevents the annotation from endorsing the stereotype as fact. It also reveals how estranged he already feels: the people are legible to him as a type before they are individuals he wants to understand. His longing to be invisible grows out of this failed contact.

notes.title: Caught between laughing and crying
notes.body: 哭笑不得 describes a situation too absurd or uncomfortable for either laughter or tears to feel adequate. Both responses are named and both withheld. Between stifling boredom and being speechless, the phrase makes reaction itself difficult: the speaker can observe the scene but cannot find a comfortable way to participate in it.

phrase.en: Don't know whether to laugh or cry

notes.title: A spectator who wants a screen
notes.body: The scene feels so strange that watching acquaintances becomes like watching another genre of reality. This is not the director’s control claimed in “Poker Face”: the speaker sits beside the action and wants nobody to address him. The film comparison places a screen between observer and participants, preparing the wish to become transparent.

notes.title: Transparency as an escape from contact
notes.body: 透明 means transparent, and the following wish explains its social purpose: nobody would stop him to talk or ask irrelevant questions. The fantasy is the reverse of demanding attention. After instructing a friend to value their existence, the speaker imagines relief in making his own presence unavailable to the surrounding crowd.

notes.title: The relief of having no role
notes.body: 局 is a situation, arrangement or game; a 局外人 stands outside it. The next identities shrink further, from an unknown little person to an unnoticed passerby. That descending list makes anonymity desirable, a way to escape being enlisted in the romances, questions and habits of a scene that already feels exhausting.

notes.title: 小人 does not have to mean villain
notes.body: 小人 can condemn somebody as petty or dishonorable, as in “Debt.” Here it is surrounded by being unknown, outside the group, and unnoticed, so the size meaning—an insignificant little person—fits the self-description better. The same two characters can serve contempt or self-effacement depending on their neighbors.

notes.title: Reassurance alongside indifference
notes.body: The earlier phrase 'pretending not to care' gives this refrain its limit. He is trying to stop other people's relationships and behaviour from becoming his responsibility. The song then returns to asking an old friend to live well, so indifference does not get the last word. This is a distinction between care he chooses and involvement he cannot bear, rather than a simple progression from compassion to not caring about anyone.

notes.title: Yang Kun’s “无所谓” is inside this refrain

phrase.en: Who falls in love with whom

notes.body: The sequence of indifference, falling in love and wearing someone down reworks the opening of Yang Kun’s “无所谓.” Here its familiar romantic resignation follows the desire to disappear from a social scene. Borrowing an already recognizable refrain supplies a ready-made way to say something the verse has struggled to express: other people’s entanglements do not have to become his own.

sources.label: JOOX: Yang Kun, 无所谓 (lyrics and credits)
CCTV: Yang Kun performs 无所谓

tracks.intro: The title's indifference is surrounded by care. A casual call becomes an earnest plea to an old friend to stay alive; a scene of exhausting social behaviour then produces the wish to disappear. 'Whatever' works as a boundary around other people's entanglements, not a statement that nobody matters. Crucially, the song returns to the friend after that refrain. Its final commitment is selective and intimate: he cannot take responsibility for every situation, but this person's continued existence matters to him.

notes.title: Too late to get an early night
notes.original: 趁闹钟还没响的时候早点睡

phrase.zh: 趁闹钟还没响的时候早点睡
phrase.en: Get some sleep before the alarm goes off
phrase.pinyin: chèn nào zhōng hái méi xiǎng de shí hòu zǎo diǎn shuì

notes.body: 早点睡 normally means going to bed early, sensible advice for a normal evening. “Before the alarm goes off” relocates it to the last scraps of a sleepless night. The everyday phrase becomes darkly comic because the opportunity to follow it has almost passed; the next insistence on continuous thinking explains why rest is so hard to reach.
notes.pinyinLabel: chèn nào zhōng hái méi xiǎng de shí hòu zǎo diǎn shuì

notes.title: Lost inside camouflage
notes.body: Camouflage normally hides a body, but writing 'lost' across it announces the inner condition. The shared opening sound of mícǎi and mímáng makes the protective outfit disclose what it should conceal. The next line insists on wear without a recognised battlefield. Before the speaker becomes threatening, the song asks us to register a kind of damage that has no prestigious event to explain it. The return to these lines later keeps that damage underneath the boasts.

phrase.pinyin: mí cǎi fú shàng xiě shàng mí máng

notes.pinyinLabel: mí cǎi fú shàng xiě shàng mí máng

notes.title: A soldier’s exterior without a battle
notes.body: 沧桑, cāngsāng, compresses an older image of seas becoming fields: a world changed beyond recognition. It describes a person worn by experience, not only by war. Translating it as “battle-worn” catches the neighboring camouflage and battlefield, but the lyric’s point is that the wear exists even without the recognized event that would explain it.

sources.label: Ministry of Education idiom dictionary: 滄海桑田

notes.title: A hard center inside fatigue
notes.body: The spine supplies a hard, upright center after exhaustion, camouflage and unseen enemies. An indestructible backbone is a bodily boast, but its placement also reads as the determination not to bend. The song moves from being worn out to imagining a part of the self that cannot be made weak, preparing the turn from inward fatigue to outward attack.

notes.title: One word moves from exhausted to destructive

phrase.pinyin: fèi le nǐ men de zuǐ

notes.body: The opening’s 废 describes feeling useless or spent; 废了 here becomes something the speaker will do to other people’s mouths—ruin or disable them. The shared word converts a state of personal depletion into an outward threat, still directed at speech rather than an identified opponent.
notes.pinyinLabel: fèi le nǐ men de zuǐ

notes.title: Huddling for warmth becomes a clique
notes.body: He attacks closed circles that protect their own, yet later speaks tenderly of how rough his brothers have it. The target is therefore not companionship in itself. It is solidarity that shields deception or keeps outsiders powerless. That distinction gives the anti-clique anger more substance than a blanket claim to need nobody. The song wants a 'we' capable of surviving dirty conditions without becoming the self-protecting group it condemns.

notes.title: Drunk with disbelief
notes.body: 我也是醉了, literally “I’m drunk too,” became a conversational expression of exasperation or disbelief: the equivalent of “I can’t even.” It lets the speaker react to something absurd by describing his own helplessness. In a verse opened by fatigue, the stock joke briefly returns the aggressive voice to being overwhelmed.

notes.title: A rich person—or a game?
notes.body: 大富翁 is both a very wealthy person and the name of property-and-money games, including the Richman series. The next line brings in anti-addiction language, activating the game association. The title “Monoplay” fits that field of play without naming a particular game. Wealth and competitive absorption sit together, making accumulation look like a pastime someone cannot stop.

notes.title: The vocabulary of stopping a game
notes.body: 防沉迷, fáng chénmí, is familiar from systems intended to limit excessive online gaming, including official rules for minors. It is not a new legal idea waiting to be invented. Following 大富翁, the phrase gives the verse’s rich people or game players the vocabulary of a monitored habit, turning accumulation into something that might need an enforced stopping point.

sources.label: National Press and Publication Administration: anti-addiction gaming notice (2021)

notes.title: A regional word for chili
notes.body: 海椒, hǎijiāo, is a regional word for chili used in Sichuan and neighboring areas. “Chili” gets the ingredient across but loses the local voice. Placing it beside kangaroo meat makes a comic meeting of the distant and familiar: an unusual food is approached with the everyday seasoning vocabulary of home.

sources.label: Linguistic study: regional words for chili peppers

notes.title: A brand name that also sounds self-absorbed
notes.body: 自嗨锅 is the Zihaiguo self-heating meal brand. 自嗨, zìhāi, also means entertaining oneself or getting excited inside one’s own bubble. Calling the meal expired makes a shelf-life judgment double as a judgment on self-absorption. Coming after the little cliques, the convenience-food label becomes a compact joke about people impressed chiefly by themselves.

notes.title: Giving up respectability first
notes.body: 无赖 can describe a shameless rogue who refuses ordinary obligations or reasoning. After condemning cliques and deception, the speaker claims the disreputable label for himself. That removes one weapon from opponents: threatening his respectability has less force if he has already theatrically thrown it away. The laugh that follows enjoys that freedom.

notes.title: Outsourcing the reckoning

phrase.en: Heaven will collect you on its own
phrase.pinyin: tiān zì rán huì shōu nǐ

notes.body: 天, heaven, acts as the eventual enforcer; 收 makes the person sound ready to be taken away or collected. Repeating this after “I don’t even have to touch you” imagines revenge without direct effort. It reprises “Cube,” where the speaker also hands punishment upward, before returning here to meticulously personalized threats.
notes.pinyinLabel: tiān zì rán huì shōu nǐ

notes.title: Changing colors as self-defense
notes.body: He celebrates being impossible to see through, then threatens to tear away somebody else's respectable cover in public. The asymmetry is revealing: concealment is protection when it belongs to him, hypocrisy when it belongs to an adversary. The song need not be a consistent moral code for this to matter. It stages the demands of a cornered person who wants control over his own exposure and over the exposure of those he distrusts.

notes.title: A threat small enough for a bathroom
notes.body: 蛾蠓 names the tiny moth-like flies associated with damp drains. After the chameleon and a threat to blind the listener, this thoroughly unglamorous bathroom insect brings the menace close to everyday life. The image does not need a large predator: something small, intrusive and difficult to ignore can already make an ordinary room unpleasant.

notes.title: An insult claimed as an identity
notes.body: 奇葩 originally names an extraordinary flower, but conversationally it often describes a bizarre person or thing. “Freak” selects that latter force. The speaker embraces the label and places himself in another world, then immediately asks whether the listener is afraid to go home. His strangeness crosses from self-description into the listener’s most familiar space.

notes.title: The audience turns against the speaker
notes.body: A podium gives someone a height, an audience and a claim to authority. The threat is to expose that person in front of children until the audience laughs. It mirrors “Sunshine” by turning an instructional setting against its authoritative figure: the person who expects everyone to listen becomes the object everybody watches.

notes.title: The cover that hides disgrace
notes.body: 遮羞布 literally means a cloth covering shame, figuratively the respectable excuse or appearance hiding something disgraceful. English “fig leaf” replaces the material image with an equivalent idiom. Tearing it away on a podium turns exposure into a public event: the person’s authority collapses not through a counterargument, but through becoming laughable before the audience.

notes.title: The problem moves from sight to survival
notes.body: Muddy water makes seeing difficult, but the line answers with the ability to breathe. That shift changes the stakes from judging appearances to remaining alive within a hostile environment. The plural “we” briefly breaks the isolated self-mythology: the following lament for “my brothers” makes survival a shared condition, not only a personal boast.

notes.title: Avoiding work by being clever about it
notes.body: 偷奸耍滑 describes using sly tricks to avoid effort or responsibility. It is not the same as the outright fraud in the parallel line about scams. Keeping the two accusations distinct makes the repeated contempt target both active deception and opportunistic evasion.

notes.title: A familiar ritual road becomes a threat
notes.body: 上坟 means visiting a grave to pay respects, rather than simply being buried. The line bends that ordinary ritual journey into an ambush-like meeting place. After saying there is a long road ahead, the speaker supplies a destination that cancels the other person’s future; the wreath and payment details then turn the imagined aftermath into a carefully managed event.

notes.title: A triumphant phrase on the wrong road

phrase.pinyin: gāo gē bù duàn měng jìn

notes.body: 高歌 and 猛进 recall the heroic idiom 高歌猛进, advancing vigorously while singing. In this funeral-bound sequence, the triumphant movement is grotesquely misplaced. A phrase suited to confidence and collective progress carries someone toward the grave scene instead, continuing the song’s habit of turning positive public language into a private taunt.
notes.pinyinLabel: gāo gē bù duàn měng jìn

notes.title: The last detail is who paid
notes.body: The repeated correction about who paid is smaller and more personal than the grand threat of death. Even the enemy's supposed tribute from loved ones turns out to depend on the speaker. He wants authorship of the humiliation, not merely justice arriving by itself. That undermines the repeated claim that heaven can handle everything without his involvement. When exhaustion returns afterwards, the elaborate fantasy has not freed him from the conflict.

phrase.en: I'm the one who paid for it

tracks.intro: Monoplay starts with someone exhausted before the alarm has even rung and ends by returning to that exhaustion. In between, he becomes an indestructible adversary of cliques, scammers and public hypocrisy. The threats give depleted energy an outward direction, but do not deliver rest. His refusal to be readable also sits uneasily beside his demand to expose everyone else. The funeral fantasy becomes obsessively personal: even when heaven is supposed to do the punishing, he wants the credit for paying for the wreath.

notes.title: “Your boy” is the speaker
notes.body: 哥, gē, is literally older brother, but as a self-reference it claims a relaxed seniority: “your boy,” with the implication that this speaker deserves recognition. It is different from the harsher 老子 later in the verse. The song can shift from teasing internet swagger to aggression simply by changing what the speaker calls himself.

notes.title: A swaggering line with an internet afterlife
notes.body: The longer slogan “don’t be obsessed with me; I’m only a legend” was already cataloged among 2009 internet catchphrases in a study hosted by East China Normal University. This line carries that recognizable boast, while the next asks to be treated as if the speaker never appeared. Legend and disappearance sit side by side.

sources.label: East China Normal University-hosted study, table of 2009 internet catchphrases

notes.title: A legend asks to disappear

phrase.en: Just act like I was never here
phrase.pinyin: jiù dāng wǒ cóng méi lái guò

notes.body: The next lines announce an entrance, so the request for erasure is not straightforward reluctance to perform. He wants to choose the terms on which his presence is available. Later, he says his story could be used against or for other people's purposes at his brightest moment. That gives the hook a concrete conflict: being seen helps make a legend, but being fully accessible makes a person exploitable.
notes.pinyinLabel: jiù dāng wǒ cóng méi lái guò

notes.title: Hollow confidence versus a solid body
notes.body: 实 contrasts with the previous line’s 虚: solid or real versus hollow, shaky, or lacking confidence. The opposition works through both the body and credibility. A few lines later, having only half a yuan still does not prevent the speaker from carrying himself with style.

notes.title: Turning a proverb upside down
notes.original: 常走在河边脚都不湿的
notes.body: The proverb ordinarily warns that repeated proximity to danger eventually has consequences. He grants himself an exemption, walking beside the water without getting wet. But the later refusal to tell his story is a precaution, which means the verse is less carefree than the boast claims. He performs immunity while actively managing exposure. The protection is work even when the persona makes it look effortless.

phrase.zh: 常走在河边脚都不湿的
phrase.en: I keep walking by the river and my feet never get wet
phrase.pinyin: cháng zǒu zài hé biān jiǎo dōu bù shī de

notes.pinyinLabel: cháng zǒu zài hé biān jiǎo dōu bù shī de

notes.title: Style without a budget
notes.body: The tiny amount in his pocket breaks the expected connection between wealth and visible confidence. This is a claim to style that does not require receipts. It also makes the later fear of exploitation more specific: someone with little money can still possess a story or image others want to use. His value in the song is not identical with what he currently owns.

notes.title: A regional question sharpens the challenge
notes.body: 咋个 is a colloquial, regionally marked way of asking “how.” 管 can mean manage, control, or interfere with someone. Here the whole question challenges the other people’s ability to police his behavior, rather than asking them for practical guidance.

notes.title: Fear of no longer counting
notes.body: 淘汰 is being eliminated, selected out or rendered obsolete. It makes the rivalry sound like a competitive process with losers who stop counting. The response is helpless anger at empty air, while the speaker watches from the side. His superiority is performed as freedom from the very contest that has made the others frantic.

notes.title: Watching drama as “eating melon”
notes.body: 吃瓜, chī guā, literally means eating melon; online it describes watching other people’s drama as a spectator. The preceding 看戏, watching a show, gives the same stance in an older image. Together they make detachment pleasurable: while the other person rages at thin air, the speaker settles in to enjoy the performance.

notes.title: Success makes a person usable
notes.body: 利用 means putting something to use and, with a person as object, taking advantage of them. The danger arrives at the point of greatest visibility, not at failure. That interrupts the earlier carefree cool: becoming more successful also makes one’s story useful material for others, giving the refusal to disclose it a protective purpose.

notes.title: A little person with a big pose
notes.body: 小卡拉米, xiǎo kǎlāmi, dismisses someone as an insignificant little character, roughly “small fry.” Its comic sound cuts the threatening social pose down to size before 社会, street toughness, inflates it again. Repeating the pairing lets the little nobody and the big pose keep colliding in the same breath.

notes.title: An intentionally elastic “society”
notes.body: 社会 ordinarily means society, but as a colloquial adjective it can praise or mock streetwise toughness. 社会很社会 uses the word in both positions, making the explanation deliberately circular: society is very “society.” Following the repeated dismissal of petty nobodies, the tautology mocks a scene whose claim to depth may consist mainly of its own tough label.

notes.title: The actual street beneath the swagger

phrase.pinyin: kēng kēng wā wā de tǔ lù

notes.body: 坑坑洼洼 doubles pits and hollows into a bumpy four-syllable texture. After the repeated grand word “society,” the verse gives us a road that still cannot be repaired properly. The mundane failure punctures the surrounding performance of power: all that talk of being streetwise has not made the actual ground easier to travel.
notes.pinyinLabel: kēng kēng wā wā de tǔ lù

notes.title: A witness who cannot be rushed

phrase.pinyin: shí jiān huì zhī dào de

notes.body: He appoints time as the witness after declining to give the current audience all the evidence. That postpones recognition rather than abandoning it. 'I know I am real' has not eliminated the wish for somebody else to know it too. The repeated promise lets him imagine eventual vindication while preserving present privacy, then leads back into the legend who both appears and disappears.
notes.pinyinLabel: shí jiān huì zhī dào de

tracks.intro: Stab wants recognition without surrendering access. The speaker makes an entrance, declares himself a legend and insists on his reality, but asks to be treated as though he never appeared. That tension becomes explicit when he withholds his story because success would make it useful to other people. Half a yuan is enough for style; the bigger risk is allowing someone else to own the meaning of that style. Time becomes the imagined witness who can eventually recognise him without exploiting him now.

notes.title: A road idiom made gruesomely literal
notes.body: The English title suggests a professional who deliberately controls a death. The opening supplies the opposite: somebody fails to notice a person waving and becomes a killer by accident. Then he hopes the victim will not hold a grudge, as though this were a minor social misunderstanding. This mismatch establishes the song's method. Confident labels keep meeting actions too careless, childish or absurd to sustain them.

notes.title: A deliberately inadequate apology
notes.body: After grinding someone to a pulp, the speaker worries about whether the victim will hold a grudge. The mismatch makes the joke: 记仇 belongs to the manageable world of social slights, and “hope he doesn’t” sounds almost considerate. Repeating the little worry lets politeness outlive the person it is supposedly concerned for.

notes.title: Flying high, drinking 高乐高
notes.body: The new-year promise to fly higher starts as ambition, becomes literal air travel, then lands in a cocoa-drink name full of the same gāo sound. The descent in grandeur is the joke. The next phone game and snack bundle develop the traveller as a child at play, not a conquering executive. Explaining only the brand would miss how the chain of sounds redirects the boast.

notes.title: Temple Run in the middle of the flight
notes.body: 神庙逃亡 is Temple Run. In his own 2025 recommendations for Perfectly Imperfect, Jackzebra said he plays it on planes, trains and before shows. The airplane routine here therefore meets a specific habit he has described. Inside the verse, the familiar phone game also helps make the grotesque road killer suddenly look like the snack-loving little boy he announces next.

sources.label: Jackzebra’s own recommendations for Perfectly Imperfect (2025)

notes.title: A branded gift pack
notes.body: 旺旺大礼包 is a Want Want assortment of packaged snacks. 大礼包 makes it a whole gift bundle rather than one treat, and 捧着 pictures someone cradling it in both hands. After the “little boy in my heart,” the pose supplies the childhood feeling through a specific, graspable object. It is snack abundance rather than a luxury-brand flex.

notes.title: Reveal

phrase.en: You won't know until I say it

notes.body: This is the first half of a conversational reveal formula: you would never know until someone said it, and hearing it gives you a shock. Its paired negatives and rhyming endings build a tiny suspense routine. Instead of delivering a grand revelation, the verse pivots into telling the listener they are too slow to keep up.

notes.title: Eliminated

phrase.en: times are going to leave you behind

notes.body: 淘汰 is elimination: an obsolete product, an unsuccessful contestant, or someone unable to keep pace gets removed. “Left behind” is gentler than that threat. After promising never to grow old, the speaker treats the listener’s slowness as grounds for expulsion from the present, borrowing the stern vocabulary of competitive self-improvement.

notes.title: School scolding

phrase.pinyin: hún hún è è bù xué wú shù

notes.body: After cherishing the little boy inside himself, he tells someone else to grow out of drifting and learn before the times eliminate them. He briefly becomes the sort of impatient adult who polices childishness. The warning then turns comically literal: fail to study, become a pig, name the famous literary pig Zhu Bajie. The lesson cannot remain solemn because association and play keep taking over the teacher's voice.
notes.pinyinLabel: hún hún è è bù xué wú shù

notes.title: From “pig” to a literary pig
notes.original: 西游记猪八戒四大名著
notes.body: Zhu Bajie is the piglike companion in Journey to the West, one of the Four Great Classical Novels. The lyric gets there by association: refuse to study, become a pig, then name a famous literary pig and the canon he belongs to. An insult turns into a miniature reading lesson.

sources.label: Hong Kong Education Bureau: Journey to the West
Education Bureau: the novel among the Four Classics

notes.title: Mind reading
notes.body: There is no mind in a roulette wheel to read. The claimed advantage therefore reveals a person reaching for control where the game does not offer it. Hard-work advice, a supernatural formula and friendly reassurance follow, each promising certainty by a different route. No win is reported. The repeated assurance that this round will work leaves us inside the act of convincing oneself, not outside it with proof.

notes.title: A familiar song title inside a gamble

phrase.en: You have to fight for it to win

notes.body: 爱拼才会赢 is also the title of the Taiwanese Hokkien hit made famous by Ye Qitian, a phrase widely used to encourage persistence. Here that encouraging motto sits after a spinning roulette wheel and “one more round,” then gives way to a spell. Effort, luck and magical confidence pile into the same attempt to win.

sources.label: National Taiwan University Library: Ye Qitian and 愛拚才會贏

notes.title: An incantation before the next round
notes.body: This formula calls on the efficacy of heaven and earth. It appears between claims of fighting to win and confidence about the next round, mixing supernatural appeal with gambling language.

phrase.en: Spirits of heaven, spirits of earth
phrase.pinyin: tiān líng líng dì líng líng

notes.pinyinLabel: tiān líng líng dì líng líng

notes.title: Sure thing

phrase.en: This round is a sure thing

notes.body: 把 counts a round or game here. 肯定行 is the certainty of “this will work,” and 稳了 just before it says the result is already secure. Repeating that confidence never supplies the winning outcome. It leaves us inside the ritual of talking oneself into one more attempt, suspended between a boast and a plea.

tracks.intro: Hitman is a sequence of comic failures of control. A supposed killer is merely a careless driver; flying higher means snacks on a plane; an inner child becomes a scolding teacher; a gambler calls chance a sure thing. The images connect through familiar sayings, sounds and everyday pleasures rather than one concealed autobiographical story. The speaker repeatedly borrows the language of mastery and then supplies details that make mastery ridiculous. The last return to snacks preserves that childish appetite instead of completing a triumphant ascent.

notes.title: Already understood

phrase.en: Now I know what you're talking about
phrase.pinyin: wǒ zhī dào nǐ zài shuō shén me le

notes.body: Sentence-final 了 makes this a change of understanding: now he gets it. But the repeated announcement is followed by “don’t give me that bullshit,” so comprehension ends the conversation instead of opening it. The refrain stages someone hearing enough to decide that no further explanation deserves their time.
notes.pinyinLabel: wǒ zhī dào nǐ zài shuō shén me le

notes.title: “Fine” turns into “go”

phrase.en: free to go where I please

notes.body: 我看行 means “I think it works.” Beside 神州 in the next line, it also recalls China Mobile’s 神州行—我看行 slogan. The verse reshuffles that ready-made advertising confidence into a boast about roaming freely. 行 xíng keeps changing jobs: approval in 我看行, movement in 任我行. The commercial catchphrase and the ordinary meanings reinforce each other.

sources.label: China Mobile: 神州行 brand and 我看行 slogan

notes.title: Missile / troublemaker
notes.original: 戴上口罩我是洲际导弹
notes.body: 导弹, “missile,” and the following 捣蛋, “make trouble,” are both dǎodàn in Mandarin. The speaker upgrades himself into a long-range weapon, then uses the identical sound to tell younger people to stop acting up. The scale jumps from military threat to scolding a nuisance.

notes.title: Age rank
notes.original: 生日比我小的别在这跟我捣蛋

phrase.pinyin: shēng rì bǐ wǒ xiǎo de

notes.body: 生日比我小的 makes birth date into rank: being born later supposedly gives someone less standing to challenge him. The line sounds like an older kid or senior colleague pulling age instead of answering an argument. That everyday pecking order gives the lone-wolf boast a small, recognizable social setting.
notes.pinyinLabel: shēng rì bǐ wǒ xiǎo de

notes.title: Hip hop test

phrase.pinyin: dào dǐ shén me shì xī hā

notes.body: Bad-faith interpretation provokes the question about what hip-hop actually is. But he does not answer with a definition; he discredits the listeners who might judge him. The argument is about who has standing to interpret his work as much as about the genre itself. That demand for interpretive autonomy makes the later question about being hated more exposed: he rejects the audience's authority without becoming indifferent to its response.
notes.pinyinLabel: dào dǐ shén me shì xī hā

notes.title: Chihuahua
notes.body: A Chihuahua is a very small dog, so the name miniaturizes the target after the speaker has inflated himself to an intercontinental missile. The next line abruptly supplies a husband who never comes home. The insult changes into a scrap of domestic gossip, yanking the inflated boast into another small, unflattering scene.

notes.title: Busy
notes.body: 忙 works first as a defense—there is no time for this—and then as self-advice: better to stay occupied. But “all excuses / all lies” follows soon afterward. The song lets busyness wobble between a useful shield and the very sort of explanation it is sick of hearing from other people.

notes.title: Face versus a line you will not cross
notes.body: Keeping public standing is described as something purchased by surrendering a private limit. This supplies an ethical basis for refusing the group: belonging can ask a person to become someone they do not respect. But the song also shows why that refusal is difficult. Being outside does not stop the desire to be understood. The later hurt prevents this compressed accusation from turning independence into an effortless moral victory.

notes.title: Sharing a nest is an accusation
notes.body: 蛇鼠一窝 puts snakes and rats in one nest: bad actors sheltering together and protecting one another. Its collective picture matters next to the lone wolf. The speaker does not reject only one enemy; he imagines a whole social habitat as corrupt and casts solitary life as the cleaner alternative.

phrase.en: Snakes and rats in the same nest

notes.title: The mask changes jobs
notes.original: 口罩我是一定要戴起的
notes.body: The first mask belongs to the boast about being a missile. When it returns, other people have become a spreading virus, so it functions as a barrier against contact. Read together, the images make isolation both a display of force and a means of self-protection.

notes.title: Why hate
notes.original: 为什么他们全部都恨我

phrase.zh: 为什么他们全部都恨我
phrase.en: Why do they all hate me?
phrase.pinyin: wèi shén me tā men quán bù dōu hèn wǒ

notes.body: The question comes directly after 'I only listen to myself'. Its placement makes the contradiction audible without any diagnosis: other people's judgement still reaches him. He can choose not to obey it and still be wounded by it. That is the emotional opening beneath the insults. The following escalation into threats answers the confusion with force, but never supplies the explanation he asked for.
notes.pinyinLabel: wèi shén me tā men quán bù dōu hèn wǒ

notes.title: A colloquial exclamation
notes.original: 我勒个乖乖当我看不见
notes.body: 我勒个乖乖 is an emphatic expression of surprise or disbelief. It is not a literal statement about a well-behaved person; “good grief” carries its function here.

notes.title: Carrying the consequences alone
notes.body: The repeated verb means bearing a load on one's shoulder. It moves the refrain from freedom of movement to responsibility for whatever happens next. After so much language about other people's corruption, the speaker claims that he will not pass his own consequences to someone else. At the same time, repeated bearing makes the cost accumulate. The lone wolf has autonomy, but no shared weight.

tracks.intro: The Lone Wolf makes independence sound powerful and costly in the same breath. The speaker refuses explanation, rejects the authority of a hip-hop audience and treats contact as contamination. Yet immediately after insisting he only listens to himself, he wonders why everybody hates him. The closing promise to carry every consequence alone is therefore more than a badge of toughness. It is the price of a position that protects him from manipulation while leaving him without anyone to share the burden.

notes.title: An anti-social social club
notes.body: The title names a streetwear brand whose contradiction is also useful here: a club formed around rejecting company. The Chinese hook rejects socialising, not society in the abstract. Yet the verse is intensely occupied with other people—what they owe, what they say, how to punish them. The repeated refusal is therefore an effort to establish a boundary that the song's own attention keeps crossing.

notes.title: Rough i
notes.body: 老子 is a swaggering, confrontational “I” here, with the underlying posture of “your father speaking.” It lets the first-person pronoun itself dominate the listener before the statement even arrives. The English uses an added swear to carry that force; plain “I’m anti-social” would lose the challenge embedded in who is speaking.

notes.title: Too much
notes.original: 知道的太多整个人都不太好了

phrase.zh: 知道的太多整个人都不太好了
phrase.en: Knowing too much has left me feeling all wrong
phrase.pinyin: zhī dào de tài duō zhěng gè rén dōu bù tài hǎo le

notes.body: 整个人都不太好了 is colloquial understatement for feeling completely thrown or overwhelmed: literally the whole person is “not very okay.” That conversational softness sits between the abrasive hook and the maxim about ignorance being happiness. Knowledge does not make this speaker masterful; it makes ordinary participation harder.
notes.pinyinLabel: zhī dào de tài duō zhěng gè rén dōu bù tài hǎo le

notes.title: Paid no service

phrase.en: take the money and do nothing
phrase.pinyin: shōu le qián bù bàn shì

notes.body: The failed paid exchange provides a concrete reason for distrust. It also exposes the disproportion of what follows: an ordinary grievance grows into an elaborate preparation of the offender's body. The recipe's exact quantities make anger feel administered rather than merely shouted. That absurd precision gives the speaker imagined control over someone who previously ignored an obligation, while taking him further into the relationship he says he rejects.
notes.pinyinLabel: shōu le qián bù bàn shì

notes.title: Twenty grams
notes.original: 再加少许蚝油和二十克香菜
notes.body: 脑花 means brains as an ingredient, and 凉拌 is to dress and serve a dish cold. Oyster sauce and an exact twenty grams of cilantro turn the threat into a usable-sounding recipe. The calm 少许, “a little,” makes it worse: the speaker handles mutilation with the practical care of somebody getting dinner right.

notes.title: Policing bad words, then uttering a curse
notes.body: He says he must keep following the person to prevent unlucky speech, then immediately delivers the enormous curse himself. The supposed reason for intervention becomes its opposite. This is not a consistent prohibition against harmful words; it is a bid to monopolise them. The contradiction makes the voice more revealing than a simple anti-hypocrisy manifesto: he is entangled in the same coercive speech he wants to suppress.

notes.title: A familiar poem takes a dark turn
notes.body: This is the opening of Du Mu’s “Qingming,” a poem associated with spring rain, travelers’ sorrow and the season of honoring the dead. A listener who recognizes it is primed for familiar verse. Instead, the next line makes the addressee’s entire family dead: cultural recognition becomes the setup for a savage replacement ending.

sources.label: Communication University of China: Du Mu’s Qingming

phrase.en: At Qingming, rain falls thick and fine
phrase.pinyin: qīng míng shí jié yǔ fēn fēn

notes.pinyinLabel: qīng míng shí jié yǔ fēn fēn

notes.title: Polite reset
notes.body: Two routine polite responses briefly reset the conversation after the family-death curse. They are followed almost immediately by another accusation of excessive talking. The etiquette sounds automatic, like clicking through an interaction, while the hostility has never actually gone away. The song repeatedly uses courteous phrasing as a hard cut rather than reconciliation.

notes.title: The mundane bill inside the confrontation
notes.original: 这么做容易耗水费电费
notes.body: After daring someone to act and invoking a society governed by law, the voice starts counting water and electricity charges. The bathos is the point: frightening conduct is measured in household expenses. It also connects back to the recipe-like threat, where mutilation came with cooking methods and exact ingredient quantities.

notes.title: Bad space
notes.body: 风水 concerns the auspicious arrangement of places. Here “the feng shui is off” comes between asking why someone has not left and telling them to go immediately. The supposedly environmental problem is effectively the other person’s presence: removing them is the proposed improvement. It is a spatial excuse for a social rejection.

notes.title: Bitter laugh
notes.body: 苦, bitter, changes what laughter means. After a ghost’s crying and a dog’s biting have reduced the surrounding company to disruptive sounds, the speaker can only laugh without pleasure. The song’s grim comedy allows the same outward noise to register both ridicule and being worn down.

notes.title: Underground, made literal
notes.body: The next line explicitly refuses the cultural meaning of underground and supplies burial in soil. That correction blocks an easy romantic reading of marginality as artistic credibility. The long vacation and little rest that follow offer deathlike disappearance as relief from disappointment. These are extreme images in the song, not grounds for diagnosing the artist. Their force is that even a flattering scene label can no longer make participation feel worthwhile.

notes.title: Little rest
notes.body: 一下下 doubles the already small interval 一下, giving “just a little rest” a soft, almost coaxing sound. But it follows “buried in the dirt,” and the next line calls the rest a long vacation. The cute diminutive and holiday euphemism make the imagined withdrawal more unsettling than a straightforward declaration would be.

notes.title: Life as a film set
notes.body: Hengdian's constructed film settings give the final illusion a physical address. After the declaration that he will speak honestly, he describes a world whose surfaces feel designed for performance. That also sharpens the opening failed exchange: people can enact a role without delivering its substance. The song wants something real behind the talk, but ends by restating its refusal to socialise rather than identifying a place where that reality is secure.

tracks.intro: The anti-social stance begins in a broken exchange: people take money and fail to do what they promised. It then traps the speaker in the very attention he wants to withdraw, devising punishments and following the offenders so they cannot speak freely. The final disappointment reaches beyond one transaction into a world that feels staged. Even 'underground' loses its scene prestige and becomes burial. The absurd recipes and polite interjections make the rage performable, but the wish for rest underneath them is bleak.

notes.title: Hurt hook
notes.body: The hook contains almost no figurative language. Before looking for a cultural code, take the complaint at its stated scale: the organ required to continue the show hurts. Repeating it makes the problem inseparable from the labour of reporting it. Each further vocal phrase is also another use of that throat. The song turns a condition usually hidden behind entertainment into the entertainment's unavoidable subject.

notes.title: Water
notes.original: 我想喝口水没人递给我
notes.body: A mouthful of water is a small, immediately answerable need. Its absence makes the later fury legible without requiring the audience to accept every insult as a fair description of other people. He is publicly visible but privately unsupported. The contrast is not fame versus obscurity; it is being watched versus having somebody notice what would help.

notes.title: Forty minutes
notes.original: 唱他妈四十分钟我好折磨
notes.body: A specific duration gives the exhaustion a clock. The performance is work that has to be sustained for forty minutes even while the throat hurts; later, time appears to slow. Instead of presenting the stage as instant recognition or escape, the verse makes the audience wait inside the performer’s bodily endurance.

notes.title: The wrong kind of audience
notes.original: 吸毒的狗逼在台下看我笑话
notes.body: 看某人的笑话 means enjoy that person’s embarrassment or failure. It is different from watching someone tell jokes. After the singer describes standing onstage and needing water, this phrase casts the crowd as spectators to his humiliation rather than people sharing his performance.

notes.title: Online stage
notes.original: 网上的傻逼随意诋毁我
notes.body: The movement from the people below the stage to the people online joins two audiences in the same complaint. In the room, they watch him fail; on the internet, they control the story told about him. The verse keeps returning to a gap between being exposed to scrutiny and being understood or cared for.

notes.title: Understanding as both language and empathy
notes.body: The first statement concerns people not understanding Chinese. Later, the language specification disappears and 'nobody understands' follows descriptions of blades and bloody phlegm. The song moves from translation to recognition: even without knowing every word, someone might register distress and respond. This is a useful limit for a listening-notes site too. Explaining the vocabulary answers one barrier in the lyric, while the lyric insists that understanding must amount to more than decoding.

notes.title: A face can “stink” without a smell
notes.original: 我的脸像木乃伊一样臭
notes.body: 臭脸 is a sour or visibly displeased face, although 臭 on its own also means foul-smelling. Pairing that expression with a mummy lets bad temper brush against a decaying body. Alongside the zombie DJ, it turns the live show into a scene of the barely animated: everyone is present, but little human responsiveness reaches the stage.

notes.title: Buddha
notes.body: When nobody in the venue responds, the appeal jumps to the Buddha. 苦苦 intensifies the pleading and carries the sound of suffering; the following polite 请问 introduces the extreme wish for the ordeal to end. The sudden devotional register makes abandonment larger than the room.

notes.title: Blades
notes.body: The sharp-object comparison tries to make an internal sensation available to somebody outside the body; blood then supplies a visible sign. Each attempt is followed by the same failure of understanding. The escalation is communicative as well as graphic: if a plain statement is not enough, perhaps this image will be. The return to the stage complaint at the end leaves the practical situation unchanged.

tracks.intro: Throat asks whether an audience can hear a performance while failing to hear the person making it. The demands are basic: water, responsiveness, relief from pain. Language difference then turns literal incomprehension into a wider failure of care. Its repetitive complaint uses the injured instrument to report the injury, so the song itself cannot fully separate expression from further labour. The imagery intensifies because each explanation seems to fail. This is a close account of a humiliating stage experience, without enough evidence to identify a particular show.
