notes.title: All the rage
notes.original: 听说现在北京流行臭虫
notes.body: 流行 describes both a trend spreading through a population and an ailment being prevalent. Putting bedbugs after it makes an infestation sound like the latest fashion. The joke is already in the first sentence, before the mock civic report begins: a thing nobody wants gets announced with the language of what is currently popular.

notes.title: Hearsay
notes.original: 他们都说是老外带过来的
notes.body: The allegation about foreigners arrives as something people are saying, inside an account introduced by 'I hear'. It is not established by the song. That matters because the voice soon claims vigilant concern for public welfare and demands an explanation. The mock report already contains an untested blame story. Its authority is part of what the shifting registers put under pressure, rather than a reason to treat its opening rumour as fact.

notes.title: Beautiful home

phrase.pinyin: jiàn zào měi hǎo jiā yuán

notes.body: The optimistic construction slogan follows bugs occupying the underside of a bed. For the pests, the home may be functioning perfectly; for the bitten residents, it is failing. That change of occupant exposes the gap between a desirable public description and the experience of living there. The subsequent building-material language makes decay sound like a successful project, repeating the same reversal of what counts as improvement.
notes.pinyinLabel: jiàn zào měi hǎo jiā yuán

notes.title: Laughing as an evasion
notes.original: 请你严肃不要跟我打哈哈
notes.body: He demands an answer instead of evasive joking, but the song later spends a long stretch laughing at an ambitious youngster. That return makes laughter more than a comic accompaniment. It is a way to refuse somebody else's seriousness and control the encounter. The speaker recognises the tactic when it frustrates his concern, then enjoys using it himself.

notes.title: A public-service voice
notes.body: 人民群众 means “the masses” or “the people”; 民生问题 means issues affecting people’s livelihoods. The formal civic vocabulary turns a complaint about bitten bottoms into a mock public-affairs report. That change of register is audible in the language itself.

notes.title: Salty food, idle worry

phrase.en: salted duck eggs, worrying for nothing
phrase.pinyin: xián yā dàn xiā cāo xīn

notes.body: The line pairs salted food with needless worry, echoing the shape of 咸吃萝卜淡操心, a saying about meddling or worrying over matters that are not your business. Here duck eggs take the radish’s place. 咸, “salty,” and 闲, “idle,” are both xián, adding a second route from the snack to having too much time to worry.

sources.label: Hu Hongxia: the saying in use

notes.pinyinLabel: xián yā dàn xiā cāo xīn

notes.title: Heads up, bottoms up
notes.body: 龙抬头, “the dragon raises its head,” names the traditional festival on the second day of the second lunar month. The next line replaces that auspicious upward movement with everyone lifting their backsides: the joke depends on hearing the two images together.

sources.label: Ministry of Culture: the Longtaitou custom

notes.title: Scrubbing away someone’s dirt
notes.body: Washing the floor can also mean whitewashing someone's conduct in online speech. The tears and kneeling make that defence costly and humiliating. Immediately afterwards, he says the stakes or opposing status are too much for him to absorb. Read together, the lines describe an unequal situation in which cleaning up the appearance of things falls on somebody with less room to resist, rather than a neutral domestic chore.

sources.label: People’s Daily: an example of figurative 洗地

notes.title: Unable to afford another injury
notes.body: 伤不起 uses the same “cannot afford it” construction as 买不起, cannot afford to buy. Hurt becomes a cost the speaker cannot absorb. 牌太大 just before it can suggest an opponent’s status or the weight of the game; after kneeling and cleaning up with tears, the admission makes an unequal encounter sound like a losing wager.

notes.title: To die for

phrase.en: So good they're to die for
phrase.pinyin: hǎo chī de bú yào mìng

notes.body: 不要命 normally means not caring whether one lives—reckless to the point of risking death—but in praise of food it intensifies “delicious.” The English “to die for” happens to preserve that exaggeration. On a track that later becomes literally invasive and violent, the disposable snack-language threat acquires a much nastier neighbor.
notes.pinyinLabel: hǎo chī de bú yào mìng

notes.title: Read the brand boundary correctly
notes.body: 上好佳 is the Chinese name of Oishi, the snack brand. The phrase divides as 换 / 上好佳的 / 也行: “switching to Oishi’s is fine too.” Reading 换上 as one verb would hide the brand name. The preceding shrimp-stick line makes this a casual snack substitution.

notes.title: Fresh info

phrase.pinyin: zuì xīn xiān de xìn xī

notes.body: 新鲜 describes both fresh food and something novel or current. After branded snacks and confidence in the taste buds, information becomes the next thing to consume. The next command switches from tasting to listening closely; the lyric moves between senses while preserving its appetite for whatever arrives newest.
notes.pinyinLabel: zuì xīn xiān de xìn xī

notes.title: Kid ambition
notes.body: 娃 is literally a child, but 你娃 can address a grown person with familiar, teasing or belittling force. Beside “look how happily you’re laughing” and the reported ambition, it makes the speaker sound like someone sizing up an overconfident youngster. The diction shrinks the addressee before the final grotesque threat.

notes.title: A swaggering “I”
notes.original: 老子喉咙里有口陈年老痰
notes.body: 老子 can literally mean “father,” but here it is an aggressive first-person pronoun: an “I” that talks down to the listener. The translation adds a swear word to carry that attitude; it is not introducing the speaker’s father into the scene.

notes.title: Aged phlegm
notes.original: 老子喉咙里有口陈年老痰
notes.body: 陈年 describes something kept for years, often valued when applied to wine or other aged products. Adding 老 makes the phlegm emphatically old and long-accumulated. After so much snack talk, this is a repulsive parody of a carefully preserved ingredient; it also brings the album’s sore-throat and spitting imagery back into the mouth.

notes.title: The last image curdles
notes.body: The gentle label follows a deliberately invasive knife-and-phlegm fantasy. Calling it postmodern tenderness does not soften the act; it shows how an impressive aesthetic description can be placed over harm. This repeats the track's earlier treatment of a beautiful home and a new mission. The ending also implicates the speaker, who is now doing the relabelling himself. The joke is not a claim that a named philosophy literally endorses this violence.

tracks.intro: Bedbug Party keeps exposing the distance between elevated language and what bodies actually endure. A pest problem becomes civic concern, collective mission, consumer chatter and finally a grotesque act labelled tenderness. The speaker demands seriousness, then contributes to the laughter and spectacle himself. Rather than supplying one secret referent for every animal or snack, follow the repeated manoeuvre: unpleasant realities acquire attractive or authoritative names, and the names do nothing to make the realities less unpleasant.

notes.title: Embarrassment
notes.body: The refrain delays saying what is wrong. Once he admits that a comfortable, quiet life feels boring, the delay becomes intelligible: he anticipates that the complaint itself will make him look bad. The song does not require a hidden catastrophe to legitimise that discomfort. Its subject includes the difficulty of speaking when one's circumstances seem to disqualify one from complaint.

notes.title: When peace feels uncomfortable
notes.body: 贱 is a harsh self-insult with meanings including “cheap” or “base.” Here the next lines explain the complaint: life is going well, yet the speaker is bored. “A sucker for punishment” conveys that self-reproach more naturally than calling him inexpensive.

notes.title: Ripples
notes.body: 波澜 are waves or billows; an uneventful life is water without a disturbance. 反而 in the next line marks the reversal: precisely because things are calm, the speaker is bored. Later the emotional “climate” becomes restless. The song shifts between wanting relief from turbulence and not knowing how to inhabit stillness.

notes.title: Morning drill
notes.original: 还不如早上起来做早操

phrase.en: get up and do morning exercises
phrase.pinyin: zǎo shàng qǐ lái zuò zǎo cāo

notes.body: 早 appears twice: get up early, do the morning exercises. It offers a repetitive bodily routine in answer to an uneventful life, which makes the solution almost comically modest. Then “hold on” interrupts it and the verse launches into artistic self-sacrifice. The speaker cannot stay with a simple plan for feeling better.
notes.pinyinLabel: zǎo shàng qǐ lái zuò zǎo cāo

notes.title: Artistic sacrifice, disreputable drifter
notes.original: 你看为艺术献身的盲流子
notes.body: The noble formula of sacrificing oneself for art collides with a contemptuous label for a drifting outsider. The next lines turn sacrifice into becoming what one used to hate. That is the real indictment: paying a high price has not guaranteed a worthwhile transformation. The song briefly looks at the artist from outside, as though the heroic story and the unflattering social judgement have become impossible to separate.

notes.title: Getting heated
notes.body: 上火 can mean becoming angry or agitated, alongside its traditional bodily “heat” sense. Here it leads into a restless climate and nerves that will not relax. The word makes the emotional condition feel heated and physical without naming a particular illness.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 上火

notes.title: Cant talk

phrase.en: I don't want to talk anymore

notes.body: He says further explanation makes him feel worse, then continues explaining. This gives the repeated hesitation a structure: silence leaves the problem unseen, while speech subjects it to more self-judgement. The endless blame that follows makes the pressure cumulative. The lyric can be candid without arriving at a clean account of who is responsible or what would repair the situation.

notes.title: Carrying the pot
notes.body: 背锅, literally “carry the pot,” means take the blame, often for someone else. 背不完 makes it inexhaustible: however much blame he takes, there is more left to carry. The same image returns explicitly as 黑锅 in “Snatch.”

phrase.en: An endless load of blame to take

notes.title: A whole life inside a dream
notes.body: The “yellow-millet dream” comes from a tale in which a man experiences an entire life of success while a pot of millet has not even finished cooking. The idiom makes achievement seem brief and unreal. After the burden of endless blame, it compresses a whole imagined career into a moment; the following death euphemism and closing eyes complete that collapse.

sources.label: Ministry of Education: 黃粱一夢

phrase.en: A lifetime of glory, gone like a dream

notes.title: A formal phrase for dying
notes.body: 撒手人寰 is a literary euphemism for death: let go of the human world. Its solemn four-character form follows 黄粱一梦, then collapses into the short, repeated command to close the eyes. The sequence moves from polished literary language to a bare bodily action.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 撒手人寰

notes.title: Changed
notes.body: Chinese can leave the subject unstated; 变了 simply announces that a change has happened. Coming after “becoming what he used to hate,” it can carry changes in the person, the life, or the whole situation without naming only one. The repeated question “what was it for?” treats the change as a cost whose purpose has become unclear.

notes.title: Two kinds of being happy
notes.body: The questions move from happiness as a feeling, to a fulfilled or fortunate life, to the ordinary check-in about how things have been. Each offers a different chance to say that something is wrong. Yet the answer is another return to embarrassment and difficulty speaking. That ending reframes the hook as a response to concern: being asked sincerely does not automatically make the answer easy to give.

tracks.intro: Self Pity begins with the embarrassment of being unhappy when life appears to be going well. The speaker cannot easily justify his distress, and self-accusation makes explaining it harder. Artistic dedication then looks less like a route to fulfilment than a process of becoming someone he once disliked. The final questions separate momentary happiness, a satisfying life and merely doing okay, but none gets an answer. The hesitation returns because the problem is not only suffering; it is how to admit suffering without feeling fraudulent or ungrateful.

notes.title: Fairytale opening
notes.body: A sunny day, nothing to do, a casual walk: the setup is intentionally ordinary and unhurried. Each short line adds one step until “I saw you” changes the attention. That simple storybook pacing makes the later animated pastry feel less like a sudden explanation than a fantasy growing out of an everyday errand.

notes.title: A pastry that looks back
notes.body: The initial 'like' permits a comparison between a desired person and a pastry; the seed eyes and wheat smell then make the pastry almost literal. Later it looks back and touches him. Keeping that border mobile matters because the encounter changes from looking at an attractive object to receiving an initiative from another presence. An annotation that chooses only a human love interest or only an animated snack would flatten the fantasy's movement.

notes.title: Seed eyes

phrase.pinyin: xī guā zǐ zuò de yǎn jīng

notes.body: The eyes are made rather than merely compared to something: 做的 turns a human feature into a baker’s small construction. Watermelon seeds bring color, scale and an edible material at once. It is an affectionate miniature image; the body is attractive because the lyric keeps noticing how it might have been assembled.
notes.pinyinLabel: xī guā zǐ zuò de yǎn jīng

notes.title: Intoxicated
notes.body: 沉醉 is literally to sink into intoxication, and figuratively to be deeply absorbed or enchanted. The next lines turn that figure into a bodily risk—one breath of the aroma could make him faint. Desire makes even approaching the window difficult, so the confident act of initiating contact has to come from “you.”

phrase.en: icing on the tip of my nose
phrase.pinyin: táng shuāng zhān zài wǒ bí jiān shàng

notes.body: He cannot bring himself to approach, so the other figure starts the contact. The icing on the nose is playful, followed by reassurance and permission not to rush. The scene's intimacy comes from being met in his hesitation rather than forced out of it. Across an album full of unwanted scrutiny and demands, this is a markedly different way for somebody else's attention to feel.
notes.pinyinLabel: táng shuāng zhān zài wǒ bí jiān shàng

notes.title: Only two
notes.original: 这间屋子里只有我和你
notes.body: The window-facing public encounter suddenly becomes a room containing only two people. That change in scale helps the reassurance land: the world outside drops away while the heartbeat speeds up. The tenderness is unusually sheltered for a mixtape so often preoccupied with unwanted witnesses, fake friends and hostile audiences.

notes.title: Taste carries the uncertainty
notes.body: The taste question tries to know in advance what getting close will feel like. Sweet and sour remain bodily flavours, but they also name the mixtape's closing and opening tracks. Here the opposition is not settled by choosing one. The repeated uncertainty becomes a small version of the encounter's larger problem: desire can bring him close enough to imagine the taste without making the outcome safe to predict.

phrase.pinyin: tián de hái shì suān de

notes.pinyinLabel: tián de hái shì suān de

notes.title: Too perfect
notes.body: 太 can intensify praise or say something exceeds a tolerable limit. Here “too perfect” prepares the final reversal: perfection is treated as evidence that a mishap is due. Even this gentle scene cannot end in unqualified trust; suspicion returns as a joke about how stories—and good days—are supposed to go wrong.

notes.title: The expected surprise
notes.original: 不出意外的话该出意外了
notes.body: The familiar 'barring surprises' formula turns into a prediction that a surprise is due. Perfection is treated as grounds for distrust. But the song does not then show a betrayal or mishap; it returns to the sunny walk and the moment of seeing the figure. That distinction matters. We hear the expectation of disappointment interrupt happiness, not evidence that the happiness was false.

phrase.zh: 不出意外的话该出意外了
phrase.en: If nothing goes wrong, it's about time something did
phrase.pinyin: bù chū yì wài de huà gāi chū yì wài le

notes.pinyinLabel: bù chū yì wài de huà gāi chū yì wài le

tracks.intro: Bakery Session lets attraction become unusually gentle before suspicion returns. The speaker is hesitant; the figure in the window notices him, initiates contact and asks him not to rush. Sweetness is therefore something offered rather than seized. But he still wants to know the flavour in advance, and perfection itself becomes evidence that something must go wrong. No actual disaster occurs in the lyric. It circles back to the first sighting, preserving both the tenderness of the encounter and the fear that prevents fully trusting it.

notes.title: A shaving cut at the imperial court
notes.body: The tiny shaving injury escalates through prestigious treatment into death, then the physicians are called performers and quacks. The joke starts with disproportion but lands on failed competence: the impressive apparatus makes the ordinary problem worse. That pattern recurs when international grandeur produces small-mindedness. The lyric repeatedly tests a large title against what happens to the person relying on it.

notes.title: Polish eyes
notes.body: 擦亮 means polish or wipe until bright. Applied to the eyes, it means become discerning and do not be fooled. The confident declaration is immediately tested by suspicious friends and a subway with no destination displayed. Across the song, claims of clear sight repeatedly run into situations whose meaning or direction remains obscure.

notes.title: Big city, small mind
notes.body: 大都市 is a metropolis, literally a “big city.” 小心眼 means petty or small-minded, literally a “small mind/heart.” Repeating 国际, “international,” makes the second line sound like another civic accolade while reversing 大, big, into 小, small.

notes.title: No terminus
notes.body: The train is ordinary urban infrastructure, but taking one at random without a displayed terminus removes the part that would make the journey purposeful. After the confident future-facing lines, this small practical absence unsettles the promise. Movement continues without a clear destination, much like the verse’s jumps between street life, secrecy and school memory.

notes.title: Salty choke

phrase.en: A little salty, a little hard to swallow
phrase.pinyin: yǒu diǎn xián yǒu diǎn yē

notes.body: The repeated 有点 makes the dinner complaint sound casual and manageable. 噎 is the uncomfortable catching of food in the throat, so the ordinary bowl of noodles adds another constricted body to this stretch of the mixtape. Its scale is deliberately small beside imperial death and an “international metropolis”: a bad evening includes something as undramatic as dinner.
notes.pinyinLabel: yǒu diǎn xián yǒu diǎn yē

notes.title: Granddad as an insult
notes.body: The following “I’m your granddad” makes 孙子, “grandson,” an insult aimed at people stealing from the speaker. Claiming the senior generation establishes a taunting hierarchy. Read together, these are not lines about a missing grandchild.

notes.title: Classified
notes.body: What must be protected is simply what he wants. Calling it top secret makes private desire sound like a state-level asset, but the following scheming and deceptive appearances give the precaution an emotional logic. Knowing the wish would give other people a way to manipulate it. This is the guarded counterpart to 'Bakery Session', where another person notices and reassures his desire instead of exploiting it.

notes.title: Plotting
notes.body: 处心积虑 describes sustained, deliberate planning with a strongly disapproving force: someone has been working out their scheme. It is heavier than a momentary bad impulse. Paired with 人面兽心, the polished four-character idioms make the distrust sound like a verdict, before the verse jumps back into a coarse complaint about money being tight.

notes.title: An animal behind a human exterior
notes.body: 人面兽心 describes a person whose outwardly human appearance conceals cruelty: a human face and a beast’s heart. The next fox-fur coat changes where the animal is located, putting it on the outside as clothing. That progression makes appearance and what lies underneath central to the passage.

sources.label: Ministry of Education idiom dictionary: 人面獸心

notes.title: Swearing inside a money squeeze
notes.original: 日子过得有点日妈吃紧
notes.body: 吃紧 means strained or in short supply; when applied to one’s days or livelihood, it suggests a financial or practical squeeze. 日妈 is a coarse regional swear inserted as an intensifier. The line’s pressure comes from the combination of a fairly sober word for scarcity and an angry spoken interruption.

notes.title: The child who sees through the costume
notes.body: The emperor's nonexistent clothing is exposed by a child, which makes the instruction to retain a childlike heart more pointed. It follows images of a human exterior concealing an animal interior and an animal skin worn as a coat. Clothing keeps failing as evidence of what someone is. The child offers plain sight in a world of elaborate presentation, though the final school memory complicates any idea of childhood as uncomplicated safety.

sources.label: Hans Christian Andersen Centre: The Emperor’s New Clothes

notes.title: Gotham in the mire
notes.body: 哥谭 is Gotham, Batman’s fictional city, whose crime and corruption are central to DC’s setting. 泥潭, a muddy pool, also describes a predicament someone is stuck in. Before the rhyme narrows to one teacher’s spit, the lyric briefly gives the everyday “same old shit” the scale of a whole corrupted city.

notes.title: Four nouns become a rhyme machine
notes.original: 至今忘不了数学老师吐的那一口痰
notes.body: The teacher's phlegm interrupts the scale of Gotham's corruption with a memory too specific and disgusting to become a heroic origin story. The rhymes then carry phlegm into guts, bad grades and an egg mouldering under bedding. Sound is visibly organising the sequence; not every object needs a separate symbolic key. What holds the passage emotionally is the reduction from public menace to a frightened, ashamed body that has not forgotten the classroom.

notes.title: Guts rhyme
notes.original: 那一口痰能让人吓破胆

phrase.en: scare the life out of you

notes.body: 吓破胆 literally makes fright break the gallbladder; 胆 also supplies Chinese vocabulary for courage. The phrase gives the ending its next detachable rhyme, dǎn after tán, phlegm. A bodily idiom becomes a sound to repeat, just as the teacher’s spit becomes disproportionately powerful in the school memory.

notes.title: Bitter grades
notes.original: 太苦了所以我的成绩烂
notes.body: 苦 can describe a bitter taste or a painful, difficult experience. Placed after the teacher’s phlegm, it keeps disgust in the mouth while becoming an explanation for bad grades. The verse turns school failure into a grotesque sensory anecdote, then lets 烂, “bad/rotten,” become another repeated rhyme word.

tracks.intro: Fox repeatedly gives ordinary discomfort an inflated public costume: a shaving nick becomes an imperial medical crisis, urban pettiness becomes international, and a private desire becomes top secret. Those enlargements promise importance without producing security. The speaker's confident future keeps meeting bad directions, tight circumstances and weary sighs. At the end, a whole corrupted city contracts into one remembered classroom humiliation. The sound-chain carries the scene onward, while the memory suggests how small bodily incidents can outlast grand claims to have moved on.

notes.title: Childish
notes.body: Calling the dispute childish gives him the position of the mature person who can decline it. But 'keep crying' later uses the very playground cruelty he claims to have outgrown. That mismatch is the song's engine, not a detail to smooth away. The refusal is itself an aggressive contribution to the argument: he withholds recognition while ensuring that the other person knows they have been dismissed.

notes.title: Everyone has an abacus
notes.body: 算盘 is an abacus, and figuratively someone’s calculations or private agenda. “Calculations” preserves both the arithmetic and the self-interest without adding a literal counting frame to the scene.

notes.title: Mock apology
notes.original: 不好意思我的野心太大
notes.body: The apology presents another person's disappointment as an accidental consequence of his enormous ambition. Yet he has just said he cannot let them get their way. The supposed accident is therefore also something he actively wants. Politeness lets him deny responsibility for a humiliation he is staging, which makes the voice more pointed than a simple statement of confidence.

notes.title: A chilled heart
notes.body: 寒心 literally makes the heart cold. In this use it means being bitterly disappointed or disheartened by someone’s behavior, rather than physically cold. The preceding mock apology makes the dismissiveness especially sharp.

notes.title: Different worlds

phrase.en: We're not from the same world
phrase.pinyin: bú shì yí gè shì jiè de

notes.body: “Not from one world” denies a shared basis for arguing. It can express incompatible lives or outlooks, but here follows “what has that got to do with me?” and becomes a way to refuse responsibility for the other person’s feelings. Superiority is expressed as distance: their complaints supposedly cannot even reach the same level.
notes.pinyinLabel: bú shì yí gè shì jiè de

notes.title: The chant turns into an idiom
notes.body: The closing expression means being unable to laugh or cry appropriately at an absurd or frustrating situation. Before it arrives, the song assigns the two reactions to separate people, then reduces them to alternating single words. Joining them finally disrupts the neat emotional scoreboard. It does not prove that he secretly cries; it makes the ending less securely triumphant than the preceding 'you cry, I laugh' routine.

phrase.en: Don't know whether to laugh or cry

tracks.intro: LMFAO turns refusing an argument into a way of winning it. The speaker calls conflict childish, dismisses the other person's hurt and then enjoys a prolonged playground taunt. For most of the song, crying belongs to the opponent and laughter to him. The ending puts both responses inside one expression of exasperation, loosening that clean division. The performance's pleasure lies in the contradiction: he will not engage, but he wants the other person to hear exactly how triumphantly he is not engaging.

notes.title: Still alive

phrase.pinyin: zhì shǎo nǐ mìng hái zài

notes.body: 至少, “at least,” sets a bare minimum after two losses: dignity and the contest are gone, but life remains. It is consolation with almost nothing comforting left in it. The following promise of starting again then takes a bitter direction: survival becomes an argument for becoming worse rather than simply doing better.
notes.pinyinLabel: zhì shǎo nǐ mìng hái zài

notes.title: Starting over

phrase.pinyin: dà bù liǎo cóng tóu zài lái

notes.body: 大不了 dismisses the worst plausible consequence: even if things go badly, you can begin again. That is a familiar resilient posture, but the next line rewrites the lesson as “this time, turn bad.” The song borrows the shape of encouragement while replacing its moral destination.
notes.pinyinLabel: dà bù liǎo cóng tóu zài lái

notes.title: One syllable changes the warning
notes.body: The near-rhyme between becoming bad and becoming warped makes a cruel choice sound unavoidable. He argues that refusing to harden will not preserve innocence; it will allow injury to deform you instead. The obedient sheep then serves as evidence. This is the speaker's survival logic under pressure, not a general truth the annotation needs to endorse. Its bleakness is precisely why the final attempt at hope matters.

notes.title: Obedience offers no protection
notes.body: The sheep was well-behaved, and was slaughtered anyway. Approval did not buy protection. Its unresolved eyes and regrets extend the failure beyond the moment of death: even the promise of a peaceful ending is missing. The passage supplies the emotional argument for turning bad, replacing a vague tough-guy instruction with a specific fear of being valued only for one's compliance.

notes.title: The eyes that cannot close
notes.body: 死不瞑目 is to die with eyes that cannot close: an unresolved injustice or regret prevents rest. Here the phrase is pulled apart around the slaughtered sheep’s eyes, and the next line spells out the regret. The image turns the ordinary praise 乖, obedient or good, into something bitter: behaving well secured neither safety in life nor peace afterward.

phrase.en: Its eyes won't close in death
phrase.pinyin: mù shì sǐ bù míng de

notes.pinyinLabel: mù shì sǐ bù míng de

notes.title: Release
notes.body: 解脱 can mean being freed from a burden or suffering, with religious uses for liberation as well as everyday ones. Here the life/death parallel makes death the animal’s only release. That bleak inversion matters to the song’s later recovery commands: the voice has to manufacture hope after explicitly depicting a world where relief arrived too late.

notes.title: Borrowed standing, manufactured credibility
notes.original: 拿着我的头号招摇撞骗
notes.body: 招摇撞骗 means exploiting a show of status or a claimed connection to deceive people. It is more specific than lying: the imposture has an audience and a borrowed source of credibility. In a verse about lost dignity and people asking to be brothers, the accusation makes association with the speaker another thing others might extract value from.

notes.title: Expression, mood and complexion
notes.body: 看脸色 means watch someone’s mood and adjust your behavior accordingly. 脸色 is also the visible look or color of a face. The next line turns that social deference into a corpse joke: a dead person cannot offer a welcoming look, and does not have a healthy complexion either.

notes.title: Brotherhood as a blame test
notes.original: 那请问这个黑锅你愿意背吗
notes.body: Calling someone a brother is tested against whether they would share the consequences. The question is deliberately costly because names and professions of closeness have become cheap. At the same time, asking another person to take the blame is a demanding model of loyalty; the speaker's injury does not automatically make every condition he sets fair. The next admission of his own stubbornness leaves room for that difficulty.

phrase.pinyin: hēi guō nǐ yuàn yì bēi

notes.pinyinLabel: hēi guō nǐ yuàn yì bēi

notes.title: Owning
notes.original: 我的固执我的偏执我都认
notes.body: He accepts the charge of being stubborn and obsessively fixed rather than claiming complete innocence. That brief self-recognition distinguishes the voice from a purely righteous accuser. But it immediately gives way to declaring everyone an enemy. Awareness of his own tendency does not yet free him from it. The closing encouragement has to work against this narrowed world, not merely follow an uncomplicated list of villains.

notes.title: Cash out
notes.body: 提现 is withdrawing a balance into usable money. It cuts through declarations of loyalty and understanding with a practical demand: make the value real this time. Across this stretch of the album, reputation, favors and brotherhood keep being tested against what actually changes hands. Here the accounting word supplies that test in miniature.

notes.title: Washing a face with tears
notes.body: 以泪洗面 is a set expression for weeping continually: tears become the water that washes the face. The later instructions to get up and discard the baby bottle extend the image into a rebuke against helplessness. The very last “I hope I’m right” then makes the promised recovery less certain than those commands sound.

notes.title: Baby bottle
notes.body: The bottle turns emotional dependence into a child’s feeding object. After ordering the listener to stop crying and pull themselves together, the speaker makes recovery sound like compulsory growing up. It is a harsh kind of encouragement: the tender infant image is introduced only to be discarded.

notes.title: Hope about hope

phrase.pinyin: wǒ xī wàng wǒ shì duì de

notes.body: The penultimate claim says the world still contains hope; the last line asks whether that claim is true. This is a real change from the opening's confident orders about what one must become. The person giving encouragement now reveals that they need to believe it too. The uncertainty here is the lyric's own emotional achievement, not an annotation's reluctance to take a position: hope survives as an effort shared with the listener.
notes.pinyinLabel: wǒ xī wàng wǒ shì duì de

tracks.intro: Snatch asks what goodness is worth when obedience has not protected anyone. Its advice to start over becomes a demand to turn bad before injury turns a person inside out. The slaughtered, formerly obedient sheep supplies the grim example; the scam and false brotherhood make the grievance personal. Yet the song finally tries to recover hope, and admits that the voice offering it is unsure. The ending is neither a clean endorsement of cruelty nor a comfortable moral recovery. It is someone trying to imagine survival without another betrayal.

notes.title: Sanmao and 3MAO
notes.original: 我有一个朋友名叫三毛
notes.body: The official production credit is 3MAO, so the name connects the song to an actual creative partnership. The detailed combat story is another matter: the lyric presents it as a friend's extraordinary portrait, not a verified biography. That distinction leaves the affection intact. A collaborator can become a martial-arts legend inside the song without every claim about training and fighting needing to be taken as documentary fact.

sources.label: Jack Zebra: official Zhuang Zhuang track list

notes.title: No knife: the empty hand
notes.body: 空手道 is karate-dō, literally the “way of the empty hand.” The name gives a compact explanation for the previous boast that Sanmao does not need to carry a knife. The next emphasis on technique rather than strength also keeps the portrait focused on acquired skill.

sources.label: Japan Karate Association: meaning of karate-dō

notes.title: Backpack
notes.original: 回国的时候只背了一个书包

phrase.pinyin: zhǐ bēi le yí gè shū bāo

notes.body: 书包 is a school-style bag or backpack, a strikingly modest item for someone arriving with lethal combat skills. 只, “only,” emphasizes how little luggage he needs. Along with the admission that he is not very strong, the image builds an unshowy exterior that the later “god of kung fu” will spectacularly exceed.
notes.pinyinLabel: zhǐ bēi le yí gè shū bāo

notes.title: Low profile

phrase.en: humble and keeps a low profile

notes.body: The friend is praised for not boasting, while the narrator boasts extravagantly on his behalf. This division lets the subject retain modesty and receive the rewards of a spectacular reputation. It is a recognisable friendship dynamic enlarged into a kung-fu story: someone else tells everyone how formidable the quiet person really is. The humour does not depend on treating the affection as insincere.

notes.title: The audience enters the story
notes.body: Recording begins before the outcome is known, and the narrator later joins the applauding 'we'. The story is assembling witnesses as well as describing a fighter. A victory becomes a public identity when others see it, retain it and acclaim it. That makes this a warmer version of the album's recurring interest in audiences: attention here helps friends build a legend together instead of exposing a performer to humiliation.

notes.title: Victory faith
notes.body: 信仰 is faith or a sustaining belief, so treating victory as its only object gives competition the seriousness of a creed. It also cuts against the friendly introductory “I have a friend.” The portrait gradually shifts from anecdote to heroic legend through the vocabulary around him, not through a detailed account of any particular move.

notes.title: Platform
notes.body: After war, faith and a martial-arts god, the applause happens on a platform. That plain transport setting brings the action back within everyday public life instead of ending in a temple or arena. The narrator’s “we” also makes the legend collective: a group has been watching and now certifies the victory by applauding.

notes.title: Quiet
notes.body: The repeated second passage stops in the solemn pre-fight atmosphere and orders quiet, rather than narrating another result. The narrator remains in charge of the audience's anticipation. After the earlier applause, this closing suspension lets the friend's reputation continue to expand in the room. The joke resides partly in how seriously everyone is instructed to receive an already extravagant story.

tracks.intro: Sanmao is affectionate mythmaking about a named creative collaborator. The friend stays humble while the narrator supplies his impossible reputation, nervous audience and godlike status. Small details—the backpack, limited strength, ordinary platform—keep the hero close enough to everyday life to remain funny. The track is interested in how a group makes somebody legendary: recording, watching and applauding do nearly as much narrative work as the fight. Its solemnity is part of the pleasure of talking up a friend.

notes.title: A family word in a nonsense loop
notes.body: 嫂子 is an older brother’s wife, or a familiar address to a male friend’s wife. Its sǎozi ending chimes with 饺子 jiǎozi, dumplings; the hook keeps moving between a woman, disappearance and dinner through sound. Later “I don’t want the sister-in-law / just the dumplings” makes a comic denial out of the resemblance.

notes.title: A grand chess game
notes.body: 下一盘大棋 literally means play a big game of chess and figuratively describes an elaborate overall strategy. Here it introduces undercover behavior, a cleaned crime scene and stories told fluently. The domestic dumpling refrain abruptly shares space with the language of a secret operation.

phrase.en: playing a grand game of chess

notes.title: Smooth story

phrase.en: Stories roll smoothly off my tongue
phrase.pinyin: suí kǒu wěi wěi dào lái

notes.body: A fluent story is called a survival skill, then placed beside a clean crime scene and an undercover identity. The sequence connects entertainment with managing what other people can know. That does not establish an actual crime; it describes a persona who wants command of the account and of the evidence. Even the nonsense refrain fits that interest in saying something memorable without making its implications easy to pin down.
notes.pinyinLabel: suí kǒu wěi wěi dào lái

notes.title: Leaving someone a handle

phrase.en: anything they can use against me

notes.body: The literal handle becomes something an opponent can grasp and use against him. Cleaning it away gives the speaker freedom from consequences in the story he tells. Later, he denies wanting the sister-in-law and insists on dumplings, withdrawing an implication the hook has repeatedly invited. The two passages share a tactic: leave the listener with a suggestive performance while denying them an easy claim on what it commits him to.

notes.title: Undercover
notes.body: 卧底 is someone embedded under a concealed identity. The image lets living “in the shadows” sound deliberate and skilled rather than merely excluded. It also complicates the earlier survival skill of telling stories: the public-facing voice might itself be a cover, while the song boasts about how little usable evidence it leaves.

notes.title: “What a talent” after a con
notes.body: 人才 usually praises a talented or capable person; on its own it can also be an ironic “what a piece of work.” Here it follows skill at storytelling, concealment and dismissing things as nonsense. The compact compliment leaves those dubious abilities intact rather than turning into straightforward admiration.

notes.title: Cat mouse
notes.body: The two short declarations assign the roles without negotiation: I am the pursuer, you are what gets pursued. Following the covert strategist, this is almost childishly direct. The song can alternate intricate concealment with a playground model of power, then immediately abandon the chase to argue about dumplings.

notes.title: Bawdy dumplings
notes.body: A circulating bawdy joke links dumplings as desirable food with the sister-in-law as a sexual object. The song can therefore activate an implication without stating it in the hook. The later emphatic preference for food is funny because the implication is already in the room. His denial is part of the play, rather than a reason either to invent a real affair or to pretend the language has no sexual background.

sources.label: Wan-Qi Li, Cyberbullying in China (2020), p.338

notes.title: Food becomes biology by sound
notes.body: 食物 shíwù means food; 生物 shēngwù means living organisms, or biology as a school subject. The shared final syllable makes “I like food / I never studied biology” feel connected by rhyme even as its logic swerves.

notes.title: What can you do
notes.body: 咋 is a colloquial “how/what,” and 你能够把我咋样 challenges the listener to produce a consequence. It is the spoken shrug of “what are you going to do to me?” rather than a request for information. The next “play all you want” formula retains that swagger while specifying a boundary around jokes at Kai’s expense.

notes.title: A circulating “Brother Kai” catchphrase
notes.body: The familiar 'play is play, fooling around is fooling around' formula introduces a boundary: do not make Kai the joke. After a track full of teasing and evasive storytelling, the asymmetry is deliberate. He claims extensive freedom to play with everyone else's interpretation, then protects his own dignity through the senior address 'Brother Kai'. The ending explains who is allowed to control the humour.

sources.label: 2019 esports fan article using the catchphrase
Apple Music songwriting credit: 张正凯

tracks.intro: Dumpling makes verbal slipperiness into a survival skill. A bawdy sound-game leads into a strategist who tells persuasive stories, leaves no evidence and chooses which remarks count as meaningless. The second verse emphatically denies the sexual implication that the hook has enjoyed creating. The final rule then limits the joke: everyone may fool around, but not at Kai's expense. The song is playful and controlling at once, granting its speaker the freedom to suggest, evade and tease while protecting his own standing.

notes.title: Posture as moral character
notes.body: 行得端、坐得正 declares upright conduct: one has done nothing shameful and can face scrutiny. After “stand high / see far,” its two clipped lines make physical posture and moral confidence share a rhythm. The speaker claims both the best vantage point and the right to judge what he sees.

notes.title: Top boy title
notes.body: Jackzebra named Top Boy among the shows he watches when discussing learning English through the internet in a 2025 Dazed interview. That gives the title a connection to his stated viewing habits. In this song, the opening claim to stand higher than everybody else also makes “top boy” function as a straightforward assertion of rank.

notes.title: Audience spit
notes.original: 观众对着你的脸吐唾沫
notes.body: The crowd supplies the opponent's humiliation while the speaker occupies the centre. In 'Throat', an audience similarly watched a performer suffer, but the vulnerable person was the speaker. Read alongside that song, this boast shows how easily spectatorship becomes a weapon when its target changes. The album does not offer one consistent position outside the cruelty of public attention; its voices can both suffer and enlist it.

notes.title: Question mark
notes.body: A question mark is something he can throw, and 接招 in the next line means receive or counter a move in a fight. Punctuation becomes a projectile. The boast is about making the other person answer on his terms: even confusion can be wielded as an attack rather than admitted as uncertainty.

notes.title: Selling a constructed self
notes.body: Selling a persona is followed immediately by fear of being forgotten. The accusation is not simply that an image is constructed—this song plainly constructs one too—but that the other person has become dependent on keeping it in circulation. Pleasing everyone then appears as the work required to prevent disappearance. The boastful speaker wants to distinguish his own authority from that dependency, though his need to compare himself keeps the distinction under strain.

notes.title: Forgotten
notes.body: The accusation against selling a persona becomes a fear of disappearing from attention. That gives the insult a mechanism: pleasing this person and that person is driven by the terror of no one remembering you. The verse presents publicity as a dependency, with the carefully maintained image resting on fragile self-worth.

notes.title: Fragility you can poke through
notes.body: Traditional paper-covered windows supply a concrete image for the previous fragile self-esteem: one poke ruins the surface. The lyric moves directly from an abstract weakness to something that can be punctured.

notes.title: A bird that repeats human speech
notes.body: 八哥 is a myna, a bird known for imitating human speech. 碎嘴 means incessant, petty chatter. Together they reduce the opponent’s voice to tiresome repeated noise; the following charge that culture is “just talk” continues that attack on speech without substance.

sources.label: Taipei Zoo: mynas imitating human voices

notes.title: Shameless, not resilient
notes.body: 皮厚 draws on 脸皮厚, a thick face: being shameless or unembarrassed when one should feel ashamed. English “thick-skinned” can praise resilience, but that is not the force of this insult. The accusation sits beside fragile self-esteem, so outward shamelessness and inward insecurity coexist.

notes.title: Betrayal as a possessing spirit
notes.original: 背刺鬼半夜上身随手做做
notes.body: 背刺 is a stab in the back, and by extension betrayal. Adding 鬼 turns the betraying impulse into a ghost; 上身 says it possesses the body. 随手做做 then treats that dramatic supernatural intrusion as something done casually. The line moves between a familiar social metaphor and a little horror scene.

notes.title: Alone again
notes.body: “Now I see clearly” leads into walking alone, a connection heard repeatedly in this run of tracks: insight costs company. But 走到哪算哪 afterward gives the independence an improvised quality—go as far as one goes, work out the destination later. The refusal to join others does not require a finished plan.

notes.title: A change in the food image
notes.body: 菜 can mean a dish or vegetables, but in competitive slang it also calls someone unskilled. 肉变菜了 keeps the literal kitchen picture—meat turning into a dish—next to the following refusal to keep playing. That juxtaposition allows competence and edibility to blur: the same word can put something on the menu or dismiss someone as an easy opponent.

phrase.en: The meat's turned into a dish

notes.title: Brothers well

phrase.en: things go well for my brothers
phrase.pinyin: xiōng dì men guò de shùn

notes.body: Happiness at his brothers' success interrupts the need to surpass an opponent. Here someone else's flourishing is not a threat. That moment prepares the warning against calling everyone a brother: the label matters because genuine mutual regard is valuable. The song is distinguishing chosen care from indiscriminate affiliation, rather than arguing that dependence on any other person is inherently degrading.
notes.pinyinLabel: xiōng dì men guò de shùn

notes.title: Heaven choice
notes.body: Heaven's will is followed by equal effort, no free reward and a decision left to the listener. The lines distribute control instead of settling on either fate or total self-sufficiency. One cannot guarantee outcomes, but can still choose where to put work and whom to trust. That practical mixture is more useful to the song's later advice than treating the heaven line as a complete philosophy of resignation.

notes.title: No free pancakes from heaven
notes.body: The proverb says that stuffed pancakes do not fall from the sky: rewards do not simply arrive without effort. Keeping the food image preserves the abrupt shift from heaven’s will to practical advice about working and deciding for yourself.

phrase.en: Stuffed pancakes won't fall from the sky
phrase.pinyin: tiān shàng bú huì diào xiàn bǐng

notes.pinyinLabel: tiān shàng bú huì diào xiàn bǐng

notes.title: Calling someone brother is a commitment
notes.original: 不要随便跟人称兄道弟
notes.body: 称兄道弟 literally means address each other as elder and younger brothers; it describes proclaimed closeness between people who need not be relatives. After celebrating his own brothers’ good fortune, the speaker warns against granting that status freely. The following “sincerity doesn’t buy sincerity” questions whether the commitment will be returned.

notes.title: Wings
notes.body: The wings are to be protected before the opportunity to fly arrives; the ideas are stored before they can be taken or exploited. These are images of preserving capacity, not just hiding from people. The final claim that school does not teach this makes the verse into an alternative lesson about creative and social survival. Its horizon extends beyond winning the present argument to remaining able to act later.

tracks.intro: Topboy begins with domination but develops a more practical argument about protecting the ability to make things and choose companions. Its adversary depends on publicity and pleasing others; the speaker wants recognition without that dependence. Genuine friends remain a source of happiness, so walking alone is not the entire ideal. Wings and a safe turn caution into preservation of future freedom. The return to the opening boasts also keeps the contradiction alive: a song warning against attention's power still enjoys demonstrating who stands above whom.

notes.title: Kowtow

phrase.en: knock your head to the ground

notes.body: 磕头 is the bodily act often called kowtowing: kneeling and bringing the forehead down. Here it is coerced submission, and later the demand continues until blood appears. Compare “Blessed,” where kneeling and joined palms ask for protection. The same lowered body expresses vulnerability there and an imposed hierarchy here, depending on who controls the gesture.

notes.title: The family tree as a threat
notes.body: Claiming to be someone’s 祖宗, ancestor, is a way of asserting contemptuous superiority. 孙子, grandson, pushes the listener down the same hierarchy. The demanded 磕头 is a kneeling bow that brings the forehead to the ground, so the language of seniority becomes a physical demand for submission.

notes.title: Raised dog

phrase.en: A dog I raised with my own hands
phrase.pinyin: qīn shǒu yǎng dà de gǒu

notes.body: Having raised someone with his own hands becomes a claim to own their obedience. The grievance is therefore more possessive than a simple demand for gratitude. Care is retrospectively recast as an investment whose return can be forced from the other person's body. The ancestor and grandson insults enlarge the same hierarchy: the opponent is not allowed to meet him as an equal, whatever their actual relationship.
notes.pinyinLabel: qīn shǒu yǎng dà de gǒu

notes.title: A head underfoot, then a ball in play
notes.body: The head underfoot slides into dribbling a ball and the claim that life is a game. The motivational 'I will not give up' now serves a scene of humiliation, rather than an admirable struggle by itself. This is one of the track's sharpest changes of moral context: persistence sounds different when the activity being sustained is domination. The sporting metaphor makes that control feel routine and repeatable.

notes.title: Sicko
notes.body: 变态 is a harsh label for someone warped or perverse. Here the speaker claims the insult himself and follows it with liking to get angry every day. That removes the expectation of proportionate behavior before the cooking threat arrives: the persona announces that excess is part of the performance rather than an accusation it will defend against.

notes.title: A real appliance brand inside the threat
notes.body: 方太 is Fotile, a kitchen-appliance company that makes range hoods. After the pressure-cooker threat, the very specific product detail makes the imagined kitchen mundane and recognizable.

notes.title: Friends, tar and anxiety
notes.original: 交友不慎焦油里掺了点焦虑
notes.body: The sound runs from 交友 jiāoyǒu, making friends, to 焦油 jiāoyóu, tar, to 焦虑 jiāolǜ, anxiety. The first two are close in sound but very different in meaning; the shared 焦 keeps the chain moving. A literal English line preserves the bizarre mixture while this note restores the audible connection.

phrase.en: mixed a little anxiety into the tar
phrase.pinyin: jiāo yóu lǐ càn le diǎn jiāo lǜ

notes.pinyinLabel: jiāo yóu lǐ càn le diǎn jiāo lǜ

notes.title: Crying and “cool” share a sound
notes.original: 哭你妈逼是不是觉得自己很酷
notes.body: 哭 kū, “cry,” and 酷 kù, “cool,” differ only in tone. The taunt turns the opponent’s crying into a question about their pose, closing the line with almost the sound it began with. The English captures the challenge but loses that tight sound reversal.

notes.title: Good fortune catches fire
notes.original: 你家祖坟冒青烟操你妈的燃起来了
notes.body: 祖坟冒青烟, blue smoke rising from ancestral graves, is a saying about extraordinary family good fortune or ancestral blessing. The second half takes the smoke literally and turns the auspicious expression into graves on fire. 燃起来 also works as “get fired up,” intensifying the collision.

sources.label: People’s Daily: the ancestral-blessing expression in use

phrase.en: Blue smoke from your ancestral graves

notes.title: Throat threat
notes.original: 救命救命你喊破喉咙都没有用
notes.body: The promise that nobody will answer a ruined throat reverses 'Throat', where an unheard performer describes pain and asks for care. Here the speaker imagines controlling the refusal himself. The connection need not establish a deliberate sequel to be illuminating: the same bodily vulnerability can be pleaded from one position and exploited from another. The album's different voices do not all occupy the same ethical ground.

notes.title: Candy
notes.body: Asking for candy infantilizes the opponent immediately after the demand for bloody submission. It suggests someone seeking a small soothing treat in a scene that offers none. The next line also refuses touch, so both comfort and access to the speaker’s body are withheld; the verse keeps all vulnerability on the other side.

notes.title: Safety mood

phrase.en: I take off the safety when I feel like it
phrase.pinyin: bǎo xiǎn kàn xīn qíng kāi

notes.body: A safety mechanism becomes dependent on how he happens to feel. That is the clearest statement of the power fantasy: no stable rule lets the other person know how to avoid punishment. The refusal of advice and unstoppable accelerator extend it. The exaggerated persona does not merely want a grievance settled; it wants freedom from limits while imposing total limits on somebody else.
notes.pinyinLabel: bǎo xiǎn kàn xīn qíng kāi

notes.title: Morgue calm
notes.original: 挡着我路的畜生太平间里焚
notes.body: 太平间 is the ordinary word for a morgue, but its written parts contain 太平, peace or tranquillity. At the end of a line threatening incineration, that placid name lands with dark irony. The verse repeatedly puts violence inside familiar rooms and household vocabulary, from pressure cooker and range hood to this final place for the dead.

tracks.intro: Kneel takes wounded pride into a fantasy of absolute hierarchy. The speaker claims to have raised the opponent, converts that care into ownership and demands bodily submission. Every possible appeal—crying, begging, asking for comfort—is denied in advance, while his own moods become the only rule. The cooking brands and sound-games make the excess grotesquely ordinary. This is a dominating persona the song stages, not a moral authority the listener has to accept. Its force includes how completely it reverses the vulnerability heard elsewhere on the album.

notes.title: A street-level warning about fighting
notes.body: The win/lose construction echoes a widely used police warning: lose a fight and go to hospital; win and go to jail. This lyric uses “pay compensation” for the winning outcome. The next “I’m not afraid” answers the warning with bravado.

notes.title: A cheerful V at an enemy
notes.body: 比耶 means make the familiar two-finger V gesture used for photographs, victory or “peace.” It is a hand pose rather than merely saying “yeah.” A bright, camera-ready gesture arrives immediately after the warning about fighting, giving the confrontation a deliberately incongruous expression.

notes.title: Medical check
notes.body: 体检 is a physical examination, but the previous line’s “fallen” life is a moral or social judgment, not something a routine health check could diagnose. The refusal makes reckless living sound like an administrative category that can simply be waved away. It belongs to the opening’s pattern of acknowledging consequences and then declaring them irrelevant.

notes.title: An “eye” for other people’s motives
notes.body: 心眼 can mean shrewdness, suspicion or a calculating intention, as well as the capacity to judge people. 没有心眼 can praise someone’s straightforwardness or expose their naivety. The next lines deliberately provoke and trample others, complicating this claim to live innocently.

notes.title: A moral line becomes a painted line
notes.body: He claims not to see a moral limit, and the verse immediately starts manufacturing visible lines in white paint. The abstraction becomes a crosswalk and then the zebra chant. That is a local sequence of language turning concrete, not just an isolated animal pun. It also suits a speaker whose deliberate provocation contradicts his claim to have no calculating angle: blindness is a performed excuse, rather than the absence of action.

notes.title: How paint makes a zebra
notes.original: 斑马斑马斑马斑马斑马斑马
notes.body: 斑马 means zebra, and 斑马线, “zebra lines,” is the everyday Chinese term for a crosswalk. The sequence paints white stripes on a street, lets them dry, then chants “zebra.” That also brings the artist’s own name into the refrain without having to say “Jack.”

notes.title: Baby home
notes.body: The repeated zebra chant suddenly gives way to a small invitation home. 宝贝 can be a lover’s or a parent’s affectionate address, without the lyric choosing one relationship for us. The softness briefly interrupts a song of fights, trampling and outrageous public declarations, before the wish for a holiday expands into collective release.

notes.title: Everyone
notes.body: The repeated “everyone” and “all” make the instructions sound universal: go play, make noise, empty the gasoline, burn the rubbish, strip and shave. Parallel grammar puts a holiday invitation and reckless acts on the same footing. The passage builds momentum by widening permission until “free and easy” slides into “lawless.”

notes.title: Lawless
notes.body: 无法无天 literally has neither law nor heaven: no human or higher authority restrains the behavior. It follows 自由自在, carefree freedom, so two four-character expressions recast the same release first attractively and then as excess. The song does not insert a clean boundary between liberation and simply doing whatever one wants.

notes.title: Reporting
notes.body: A person who just declared freedom from law suddenly reports upward and formally applies for an appliance. The shift makes authority a role he can enter or leave by changing his diction. That matters more than assigning every passage to one stable speaker such as a specific official. The song is playing the formats themselves, letting a command, an application and a notification each momentarily organise the world.

notes.title: Money needs washing
notes.body: A washing machine follows the complaint about earning too much money. 洗钱 is the Chinese term for money laundering, literally “wash money”; putting an actual washer beside the money makes that figurative verb into a domestic appliance joke.

notes.title: Needs
notes.original: 保障每个人的生活需求

phrase.zh: 保障每个人的生活需求
phrase.pinyin: bǎo zhàng měi gè rén de shēng huó xū qiú

notes.body: The promise to meet everyone's needs turns into a plan for a highly rated tourist attraction. Care for people and promotion of a place occupy the same reassuring register, although they are not the same achievement. The payment that follows then proves to be game money. Across the sequence, impressive language keeps offering value whose practical substance disappears when somebody tries to receive it.
notes.pinyinLabel: bǎo zhàng měi gè rén de shēng huó xū qiú

notes.title: Five A’s is an official tourism grade
notes.original: 目标是打造成著名的5A级景区
notes.body: 5A is the highest grade in China’s national tourist-attraction rating system. The line adopts development-plan language—“the goal is to build”—then follows it with a formal welcome to auspicious land. The precise grade gives the grand promise the sound of tourism promotion.

sources.label: Ministry of Culture and Tourism: 5A is the highest grade

notes.title: Auspicious land
notes.original: 欢迎来到这片风水宝地
notes.body: 宝地 is a treasured or excellent place; 风水 makes its excellence auspicious, favorable to those who occupy it. The formal 您好 and 欢迎 imitate a host welcoming visitors. After the crosswalk’s plain painted street, the speaker has verbally upgraded the location into somewhere that can be sold as special.

notes.title: From official welcome to notification
notes.original: 您有一笔待接收的转账
notes.body: The polite 您 and “a transfer waiting to be accepted” read like a payment notification. 举报 then abruptly turns reception into a complaint: the money is only game currency. The short labels 报告, 提醒, 举报 and 遗言 make the verse keep changing its format, from report to alert to accusation to last words.

notes.title: Final apology
notes.original: 给大家添麻烦了对不起

phrase.pinyin: gěi dà jiā tiān má fán le

notes.body: The heading 'last words' gives an ordinary apology an extreme setting. The person who began by dismissing consequences now imagines leaving behind inconvenience for the group. But the track then returns to the opening boast rather than ending at this confession. It cycles through a moment of social obligation and back into bravado, leaving neither the fearless persona nor the apologetic one as its sole identity.

tracks.intro: Crosswalk keeps changing the format in which a person can speak: warning, provocation, collective permission, official application, tourist welcome, payment alert, complaint and last words. Each format briefly supplies authority before the next punctures it. The money becomes game currency and the fearless troublemaker becomes someone apologising for inconvenience. Painted street markings bring the sequence back to a visible line and to Zebra's name. The song enjoys how easily language can manufacture a grand scene, while repeatedly exposing the flimsy material underneath.

notes.title: Lemon water
notes.body: The line sounds like a manageable piece of self-care advice wedged between bad luck and the fear of getting old. Its modest scale matters: the speaker can choose what to drink even though the passage soon expands into loneliness, aging and worry. The title’s cheerful beverage holds a much less cheerful routine.

notes.title: Old age and childhood share the verse
notes.body: The lyric moves from not wanting to age into supplements, absent adult children and saving for the future, then looks back to childhood on a school bus. That temporal movement is in the text; it gives the repeated security-booth scene more than one stage of life to resonate against.

notes.title: Complaints
notes.body: 满嘴 literally fills the mouth; 牢骚 are grievances and grumbling. The next “unpleasant smell” gives that verbal bitterness a sensory presence, followed by “no antidote.” The opening makes resentment feel like something one carries in the body, while “bitter smile” returns the whole sequence to the language of taste.

notes.title: Security booth
notes.body: The booth, fan and hand-held walnuts make a stationary refrain while the verses move through whole stages of life. That contrast gives passing time a physical form: the small routine continues while children leave and childhood becomes memory. The lyric never names the sitter or says this is Jackzebra's employment history. Its power lies in the recognisable scene's ability to hold an imagined future and an observed older life together.

notes.title: Walnuts for the hands, not the mouth
notes.body: 盘核桃 means repeatedly turning and rubbing ornamental walnuts in the hand, often a carefully matched pair. The hard shells change color and develop a patina through handling. Here the movement joins a fan in a security booth: a tiny, repeating routine for passing time. The nuts are being worked on rather than eaten, an important distinction in this food-filled record.

sources.label: Beijing Forestry and Parks Bureau: ornamental walnuts

notes.title: Children away
notes.body: Cash answers the practical problem of old age immediately after the absence of children raises an emotional one. The juxtaposition does not say money is useless; the later budget shows why it matters. It shows that provision and companionship meet different needs. The person can prepare responsibly for survival and still have nobody nearby to share the day.

notes.title: Younger treasures
notes.body: Calling the younger generation treasures complicates the earlier portrait of a small-minded complainer. The same person can be bitter in manner and generous in attachment. Saving the larger share while living on the smaller one gives that care a material cost. The song does not make the character lovable by removing the irritation; it lets us hear what the irritating surface fails to disclose.

notes.title: The big share and the small share
notes.body: 大头 and 小头 literally mean “big head” and “small head,” but here mean the larger and smaller portions of money. Most is saved for the future; the remainder meets 温饱, the basic needs of food and clothing. Translating them as body parts would obscure this ordinary budgeting vocabulary.

notes.title: Childhood future
notes.body: The future just described involves old age, budgeting and absent children; now the lyric returns to a child who looked toward the future eagerly. That reversal changes what “a fulfilled life” might mean. The adult’s effort to leave no regrets is heard beside the younger self who did not yet know how brief the shared happiness would be.

notes.title: Different stops
notes.body: The shared bus ride ends because people have different homes, not because someone necessarily betrays anyone. This is an important alternative to the album's many hostile explanations of separation. Ordinary destinations are enough to dissolve a temporary community. Coming after a life spent saving for the future, the memory asks what is lost when the warmth of being together is always understood as something that can wait.

notes.title: A bus full of separate destinations
notes.body: 各回各家、各找各妈 is a playful rhyming way to tell a group to disperse: everyone go home, everyone find their own mother. After the school-bus image, its singsong 家 jiā / 妈 mā rhyme sounds childlike, while the different stops give that shared journey an ending.

phrase.en: Everyone goes to their own home

tracks.intro: Lemonade imagines aging through small routines rather than a grand life summary. The grumbling figure in the security booth is also someone who misses absent children, cherishes younger people and saves more than they spend on themselves. A childhood bus ride then puts the hoped-for future beside the separations that future contains. The fear is not just looking old; it is spending a life postponing comfort, worrying and losing shared time. Irritability and tenderness belong to the same portrait, without requiring the character to be a literal biography.

notes.title: Drifting gives way to confrontation
notes.body: Doing nothing initially feels good. The clipped list then introduces exhaustion, bad mood and a demand not to be looked at. The later explanation of humiliating social effort changes how we hear the opening: drifting is a pleasure, but also relief from encounters that cost more than they return. Neither pure laziness nor pure suffering captures the movement between those states.

notes.title: A stance of not taking things seriously
notes.body: 吊儿郎当 describes a careless, unserious way of behaving, often with a judgment that someone is shirking responsibility. Here the speaker adopts that description himself and immediately says it feels great. It makes the opening’s inactivity sound like an embraced attitude rather than just a lack of energy.

notes.title: Meditation
notes.body: An empty head and closed eyes can be framed as doing nothing or as deliberate meditation. The isolated word briefly gives the slacking a more elevated name. The next explanation, though, is simply that there is a bed in his room. The sequence keeps collapsing lofty reasons for withdrawal into the immediate appeal of being comfortable.

notes.title: Bed escort
notes.body: The bed helps him into sleep reliably and on time. The personification supplies a small model of dependable care before the verse describes people whose words cannot be trusted. An object does not make him audition for its warmth or repay a social debt. That contrast explains the attraction of staying in more precisely than a generic dislike of going outside.

notes.title: Playing dumb
notes.body: 装 means put on an appearance, so this is a performed stupidity rather than an admission of not understanding. The clipped list around it—no energy, bad mood, don’t look at me—makes refusal feel like a status update. Withdrawal is presented through small, self-contained responses that discourage anyone from asking for more.

notes.title: A warm face meets a cold backside
notes.body: The warm face pressed against a cold backside makes unanswered friendliness bodily humiliating. He also says they barely know each other, so the issue is not necessarily a lost intimate bond. It is the expectation that he should perform eagerness without reciprocal welcome. Refusing that performance protects dignity, even as the later generalisation that everyone conceals something hardens a particular frustration into suspicion of the whole scene.

notes.title: A baffling “move”
notes.body: 操作 means an operation or the way someone handles something. Calling it 谜一般, “like a mystery,” is a sarcastic way to say someone’s behavior makes no sense. “Move” carries that judgment.

notes.title: A hidden motive, pictured inside the body
notes.body: 心怀鬼胎 literally imagines harboring a ghostly fetus in one’s heart. As an idiom it means concealing a bad intention or ulterior motive. “Something to hide” carries the accusation.

notes.title: Social steps

phrase.en: Their social steps are so assured
phrase.pinyin: shè jiāo de bù fá hěn wěn jiàn

notes.body: 稳健 normally praises steady, sound progress. Applied to socializing immediately after “hidden motives,” that positive vocabulary turns suspicious: these people move through relationships too competently to seem innocent. The next storm reveals their faces. The worry is that polished social ease helps conceal what a person will do when circumstances change.
notes.pinyinLabel: shè jiāo de bù fá hěn wěn jiàn

notes.title: Words that do not count as a promise
notes.body: 说话算话 means that what you say counts: you keep your promises. Negating it repeats 话, “words,” around the failure to follow through. The later demand for 真心话, honest words, tightens the complaint from unreliability into a test of sincerity.

notes.title: Honest words
notes.original: 不说真心话的小崽子会被我打
notes.body: The demand for words from the heart ends in a threat to hit whoever withholds them. That cannot secure the sincerity it wants: frightened people have a new reason to say what will satisfy the threatening person. The contradiction is a destination of the song, not a loose end the annotation should repair. The speaker who wanted freedom from social demands has begun issuing a particularly forceful one himself.

tracks.intro: Rabbit begins by celebrating inactivity, then exposes the effort underneath avoiding people. A bed is reliable, while social warmth can be unreturned and confident manners can conceal bad intentions. The speaker's retreat therefore protects both comfort and dignity. But the ending reverses his opening wish to be left alone: he demands truth from others under threat. The song traces how disappointment can turn a desire for less contact into a desire to control the contact that remains, without making that demand a solution to mistrust.

notes.title: Cant bother
notes.body: 懒得 is unwillingness to spend effort, not necessarily inability. Repeating it for listening and caring makes disengagement sound like an allocation of time: this exchange is not worth the work. That claim gets tested when the speaker admits the others have made enough trouble that he has to push himself again.

notes.title: Act together

phrase.en: put on an act with you

notes.body: The refusal is to act with the person, not simply to watch them. A convincing social performance often requires somebody else to accept the role assigned to them: grateful beneficiary, loyal associate, impressed audience. The old operator's skill matters only if the speaker supplies that cooperation. Repeating 'no time' is a way of withdrawing it, although the verse admits that the disruption still forces him to spend effort.

notes.title: An old fried-dough stick
notes.body: 老油条 is literally an old youtiao, the fried dough often eaten with soy milk. Figuratively it is a practiced operator: someone who knows the ropes and has become slippery with experience. The title keeps the breakfast pairing audible behind the insult. “Brilliant acting” then specifies the skill this particular old hand has acquired: appearing convincing.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 老油條
Kinmen Daily: youtiao, soy milk and the figurative insult

notes.title: A favor becomes a debt
notes.original: 我可不想欠你一个人情

phrase.pinyin: qiàn nǐ yí gè rén qíng

notes.body: The worry is about owing this particular person, after recognising their acting skill. A favour can create an expectation that later limits what the recipient may refuse. Declining it is therefore not an abstract rejection of generosity. It is a judgement about the terms under which apparent help arrives. The track makes a social obligation visible before it has been accepted, while 'Debt' explores the exhausting work of collecting obligations afterwards.
notes.pinyinLabel: qiàn nǐ yí gè rén qíng

notes.title: Dog chocolate
notes.original: 你是条狗吃巧克力会死
notes.body: The insult pretends to offer protective advice: because the listener is a dog, a tempting food is dangerous to them. That combines exclusion with mock concern—something desirable exists, but not for you. The following direction to find somewhere cool repeats the maneuver, wrapping “get lost” in language that sounds superficially considerate.

notes.title: “Go somewhere cool” means go away

phrase.en: Go find somewhere cool and stay out of my way
phrase.pinyin: nǎ liáng kuài nǎ dāi zhe qù

notes.body: 哪凉快哪呆着去 is a dismissive way to tell someone to get lost or stop bothering you. Literally it offers somewhere cool to sit, disguising the rejection as an almost hospitable suggestion. After the dog-and-chocolate insult, the surface concern keeps turning into exclusion.
notes.pinyinLabel: nǎ liáng kuài nǎ dāi zhe qù

notes.title: Poached chicken
notes.body: 白切鸡 is chicken gently cooked and then cut for serving; the dish name makes the animal ready for a table. The next line imagines its defiant mouth while alive, then praises the firmness of its meat. The passage changes the target from a person who can argue back into something the speaker can inspect and consume.

notes.title: A hard mouth becomes tough meat
notes.body: 嘴硬 means talking tough, refusing to concede or admit fault. Giving that “hard mouth” to a chicken before describing its firm meat pulls an idiomatic personality trait back into the body. The animal insult becomes kitchen imagery.

notes.title: Focus elsewhere
notes.original: 我的重心早放在了别处
notes.body: He claims that his attention moved on long ago, then continues by warning a newcomer about the person. That continuation gives his involvement another possible purpose besides winning his own quarrel. Even if he wants out, he does not want someone inexperienced to mistake the performance for trustworthy care. The song's indifference is selective: it refuses a manipulator while still spending words on the person who could be taken in.

notes.title: A newcomer leaving the thatched cottage
notes.body: 初出茅庐 literally means first leaving a thatched cottage. The idiom comes through Romance of the Three Kingdoms and Zhuge Liang’s entry into service; in everyday speech it describes someone inexperienced and just entering the wider world. Here the next line strips away any expectation of gentler treatment for a beginner.

sources.label: Ministry of Education idiom dictionary: 初出茅廬

notes.title: No handicap

phrase.en: Nobody's going to go easy on you
phrase.pinyin: méi rén huì ràng zhe nǐ

notes.body: 让着 someone means give them room, hold back, or let them have the advantage, often out of kindness or because they are younger. Its negation cancels the customary excuse of inexperience. After the literary 初出茅庐, the sentence lands as plainspoken instruction about entering a competitive social world.
notes.pinyinLabel: méi rén huì ràng zhe nǐ

notes.title: Their calculations line up
notes.body: The shared sky and dream initially promise common purpose. What turns out to be synchronized is each person's private calculation. The abacus makes self-interest audible as a collective rhythm: people can move together without actually caring for one another. This closes the verse's argument about acting and favours. Agreement on a reassuring public story is not proof that the underlying obligations are mutual.

tracks.intro: Soymilk treats a favour as a possible trap rather than automatic kindness. The slick operator wants a co-performer, and the speaker's repeated refusal is an attempt to withhold the participation that makes the act work. Yet trouble draws him back, and he turns toward warning someone less experienced. The final shared dream becomes synchronized self-interest. Beneath the food jokes is a practical question: when people offer connection, what obligations and performances are they asking you to accept along with it?
