notes.title: Beheading

phrase.en: every one of them should be beheaded
phrase.pinyin: gè gè dōu děi kǎn tóu

notes.body: 砍头 is an execution by cutting off the head. In a track that crowns its speaker emperor, it helps establish the theatrical role: he pronounces a collective sentence before arguing the case. The specificity makes the monarchy more than a generic rap rank. He performs the ruler’s supposed right to punish, then later sabotages his own exemption.
notes.pinyinLabel: gè gè dōu děi kǎn tóu

notes.title: Words and music
notes.body: Naming words and composition claims the whole song as something others want to take. That specificity makes the later confession of being a thief more than a random self-insult. He has defined the grievance carefully before adding himself to the category. The song does not establish that every influence is equivalent to every act of copying; it prevents the accuser from occupying a perfectly untouched position outside circulation and borrowing.

notes.title: Deluded hope
notes.body: 痴心妄想 dismisses a desire as foolish and unrealizable, more contemptuous than ordinary hopeful thinking. The little 有点, “a bit,” understates that rejection, making it sound casually devastating. This mock moderation is one of the song’s tools: he can order heads cut off, then act as if he is only offering a mild assessment of bad judgment.

notes.title: Bouncy insults
notes.body: 空空的, 麻麻的, 假假的, 瞎瞎的 and 丑丑的 give each insult the same doubled shape: empty, numb, fake, blind, ugly. Several also share the broad a vowel, helping the list fall into a taunting sing-song pattern. The childish simplicity is part of the insult. He reduces the rivals to a row of defective body parts and appearances rather than granting them an argument.

notes.title: Uneducated, uncultured
notes.body: 没有文化 commonly means lacking education, knowledge or cultivation. It does not mean having no cultural identity. Here the phrase is used as a mock excuse for swearing, immediately after a deliberately repetitive chain of insults. He adopts the judgment that might be made about his speech and turns it into permission to continue speaking that way.

notes.title: The emperor is made of the same stuff

phrase.pinyin: wǒ men dōu shì ní bā

notes.body: The first-person plural levels everybody into the same material in hip-hop's soil. It briefly contradicts the imperial arrangement in which one person stands above the rest and orders their punishment. The final 'also' returns to this inclusive gesture. The shared material does not stop competition, but it makes the fantasy of a ruler entirely self-created and separate from the field harder to sustain.
notes.pinyinLabel: wǒ men dōu shì ní bā

notes.title: Invite abuse

phrase.en: You can come curse me out now
phrase.pinyin: nǐ men kě yǐ lái mà le

notes.body: The speaker gives critics permission to begin, as though their reaction were another stage he has already scheduled. This is defensive control through anticipation: an insult loses some surprise when it arrives on cue. It also makes the “just playing” claim double-edged—he withdraws seriousness at the same moment he invites a contest over it.
notes.pinyinLabel: nǐ men kě yǐ lái mà le

notes.title: Serious joke

phrase.pinyin: fǎn zhèng dōu shì xiào huà

notes.body: Calling everything a joke gives him an exit from criticism while he continues repeating the theft accusation. The investment has not vanished just because seriousness is disclaimed. This is a familiar strategy elsewhere on the album: anticipate the objection, name the performance as play, and keep enjoying its force. The listener does not have to choose between total sincerity and total irony to hear the grievance working.
notes.pinyinLabel: fǎn zhèng dōu shì xiào huà

notes.title: His own earlier title
notes.body: 王中王 is the title of an earlier Jackzebra mixtape, so the boast refers back to a name already attached to his work. The line treats the catalog as a ladder of ranks: an existing king-of-kings title can be surpassed by a fresh emperor title. Its “last year / this year” contrast is the speaker’s promotional flourish, not a reliable dating guide for the whole tape.

notes.title: A bigger crown
notes.body: The promotion is self-announced and repeated until it becomes a chant. Its grand names also belong to familiar meat products, keeping the coronation close to the album's food-filled everyday world. The final thief confession then removes the new emperor's exemption from his own accusation. The performance can enjoy superiority while building the means to puncture it into the same verse.

sources.label: 皇上皇: official brand and product site

notes.title: Royal names on the supermarket shelf
notes.body: Both royal names also belong to meat products: Shuanghui sells 王中王 sausage, while 皇上皇 is a Cantonese cured-meat brand. That everyday commercial layer makes the promotion funnier in Chinese. He can sound as if he is ascending above every ruler while also moving between names familiar from food packaging. The wordplay punctures grandeur without requiring the boast to stop.

sources.label: 皇上皇: official brand and product site

notes.title: Also thief

phrase.pinyin: wǒ yě shì yí gè xiǎo tōu

notes.body: 'Also' adds him to the opening category rather than declaring that theft never happened. That is a more difficult ending than either denying the grievance or maintaining perfect innocence. His work, too, exists among inherited phrases, references and styles. The final repeated theft syllable lets the emperor relinquish the distance from his subjects without turning the song into a tidy rule about which kinds of borrowing are acceptable.
notes.pinyinLabel: wǒ yě shì yí gè xiǎo tōu

notes.title: Stealing and sneaking

phrase.en: Steal, steal, steal, steal, steal, steal
phrase.pinyin: tōu tōu tōu tōu tōu tōu

notes.body: 偷 means steal; 偷偷 means secretly or stealthily. A long unbroken string of the character keeps both readings available on the page after the confession. The repeated syllable also abandons the earlier distinctions between lyrics and music for the bare act itself. English “steal, steal” catches the chant but loses the doubled word hiding inside it.
notes.pinyinLabel: tōu tōu tōu tōu tōu tōu

tracks.intro: Emperor performs an authority it ultimately refuses to keep innocent. The speaker condemns stolen lyrics and music, excuses his own abuse as uncultured play, promotes himself above kings, then joins the thieves. Shared mud and the meat-brand echoes have already undermined the coronation from within. The ending does not make his grievance meaningless; it makes ownership and originality harder to claim from a position of purity. The ruler's theatrical sentence returns to include the person pronouncing it.

notes.title: Warning
notes.body: 下场 is an outcome with a punitive shade: what becomes of somebody after an action. The opening connects it to not following another person’s instructions, then says the lesson has already been experienced. Before the ambition and self-confidence arrive, the song establishes a voice that remembers disobedience as something with a price.

notes.title: Bitter echo

phrase.en: The bitterness echoes on and on.
phrase.pinyin: kǔ wèi huí dàng yōu cháng

notes.body: Taste is described through duration and sound: bitterness reverberates. 苦 can already mean suffering as well as bitter flavor, so the line makes an unpleasant experience remain sensory after it is over. Its return before the new verse prevents the later efforts toward perfection from sounding untouched by what happened earlier.
notes.pinyinLabel: kǔ wèi huí dàng yōu cháng

notes.title: Headlong
notes.body: The method is collision while the desired result is flawlessness. He tries every available move and angle, but constant activity does not establish control. The opening memory of punishment for disobedience puts additional pressure behind the pursuit: getting the self right already has consequences attached. That combination prepares the later public image as something worked at intensely, rather than a effortless expression of confidence.

notes.title: Every move he knows
notes.body: 解数, pronounced xièshù in this expression, is a repertoire of moves or techniques; 浑身解数 puts the whole body’s resources into use. “Every trick” here is every available skill, not necessarily deception. The phrase adds bodily effort to the claim of trying different angles, just before that same body becomes unable to withstand attention.

notes.title: Nothing in one’s eyes
notes.body: 目中无人 literally places nobody else in one’s eyes: treating other people as beneath notice. A few lines later everyone’s gaze and the camera are fixed on him. That reversal changes who controls looking. The posture of ignoring others does not stop being exposed to them, and the bright attention soon becomes physically destructive.

notes.title: Quiet visible

phrase.pinyin: hěn níng jìng hěn gū dú

notes.body: Quiet loneliness comes directly before being watched by everyone. The two conditions coexist. Attention supplies exposure without necessarily supplying somebody who can respond when help is needed; the unreachable ice bucket makes that failure concrete. The song's problem is therefore not solved by simply becoming more visible. Visibility is already abundant, and soon becomes the threatening force itself.
notes.pinyinLabel: hěn níng jìng hěn gū dú

notes.title: Bright light
notes.body: 打光 is setting or throwing light for a camera, a practical term from image-making. The next line turns that artificial light into sunlight heating the body. The shift is the hinge of the transformation: a professional condition of being seen becomes an elemental force, making the later snowman image feel earned by the sequence.

notes.title: Ice bucket
notes.original: 冰桶就在眼前我却够不到

phrase.zh: 冰桶就在眼前我却够不到
phrase.en: The ice bucket is right in front of me, but I can't reach it.
phrase.pinyin: bīng tǒng jiù zài yǎn qián wǒ què gòu bú dào

notes.body: Relief is not distant or invisible; it is right in front of him. 够不到 specifically makes it beyond the reach of the body. That is a sharper frustration than simply being overheated: the scene supplies a recognizable solution while withholding the ability to use it. The subsequent discovery that he is a snowman makes the urgency retroactive.
notes.pinyinLabel: bīng tǒng jiù zài yǎn qián wǒ què gòu bú dào

notes.title: Becoming a snowman
notes.body: The delayed discovery that he is a snowman reorganises the earlier scene. The camera's flattering brightness, sunlight and inaccessible ice now belong to one threat. What would help an ordinary performer be recognised destroys the form of this performer. The metaphor is unusually exact: attention and erasure are not opposite stages of a career here, but linked effects of the same exposure.

notes.title: Weightless

phrase.en: stop feeling the weight of my body
phrase.pinyin: gǎn shòu bú dào shēn tǐ de zhòng liàng

notes.body: Losing weight could have sounded like release from the tape’s many burdens, but here it marks physical disappearance. The snowman does not become freer; he loses the form by which he could be recognized. The line turns lightness into another danger, complicating the usual contrast between oppressive weight and welcome relief.
notes.pinyinLabel: gǎn shòu bú dào shēn tǐ de zhòng liàng

notes.title: The long river of history
notes.body: 历史长河 is the familiar “long river of history,” an expansive image for time and collective memory. His melted body enters it as an unrecognizable puddle. The grand scale does not preserve him; it dissolves his identity further. The next line states the fear plainly: the name and person may be lost even if some material trace remains.

notes.title: A bewildered morning
notes.body: 懵逼 is coarse, colloquial language for being completely stunned or confused. It breaks the elevated “river of history” register with an everyday, profane morning. “What the fuck” keeps that rupture in English. The phone then rings as if an ordinary day can resume, though the preceding scene has just made an ordinary, stable self difficult to take for granted.

notes.title: A new self for the morning

phrase.en: who I want to become today
phrase.pinyin: jīn tiān xiǎng biàn chéng shuí

notes.body: The caller asks who he wants to become, rather than what he plans to do. After the melting sequence, identity itself appears as something required anew for the day's activity. The question leaves room for possibility, but its repetition also makes that possibility sound compulsory. No new self is chosen in the lyric. The song ends with the request still ringing, not with a completed rebirth.
notes.pinyinLabel: jīn tiān xiǎng biàn chéng shuí

tracks.intro: Morning makes being seen the cause of disappearing. The speaker tries to produce a flawless self, draws the camera's attention and discovers that the light is melting a body made of snow. Even relief is visible but unreachable. Once the self has dissolved into an anonymous historical current, an ordinary phone call asks who he wants to become today. The question could offer reinvention, but after the preceding loss it also sounds like another demand to supply a presentable identity before the day can begin.

notes.title: A little quiet
notes.body: The repeated verb asks for a little settling or quiet, not necessarily permanent isolation. That modest request matters before the title's large imperative. The person needs enough space from other people's words to hear and answer their own situation. Rest and continuation are not treated as automatic opposites: a boundary around attention can be part of what makes further action possible.

notes.title: Pronoun dialogue

phrase.en: How can you still not believe it?
phrase.pinyin: nǐ zěn me hái bù xìn

notes.body: The opening “I” becomes “you” as the song starts asking questions. It can sound like self-address, an inner voice impatient with the person who keeps being surprised by the same world. The change lets the lyric stage disagreement without introducing another named character. The refrain then answers that questioning voice with an instruction rather than an explanation.
notes.pinyinLabel: nǐ zěn me hái bù xìn

notes.title: Accepting one’s lot
notes.body: The lyric first demands that the listener believe reality is cruel, then challenges the conclusion that they must accept their allotted fate. Recognition and resignation are different acts. This also reopens the ending of 'Life Life Life', where fate had to be accepted. The album can contain both formulas because they are positions voiced under different pressures, rather than chapters in one consistently stated doctrine.

notes.title: Perseverance repeat

phrase.en: Keep going, keep going to the end.
phrase.pinyin: jiān chí jiān chí dào dǐ

notes.body: 坚持 is holding on or persisting; 到底 adds carrying it through to the end. Repetition turns the advice into an action the song can perform: it keeps saying keep going. But no destination or reward is specified. The commitment is to continuation itself, contrasting with “All In,” where making it big is the explicit condition of going home.
notes.pinyinLabel: jiān chí jiān chí dào dǐ

notes.title: Still strength

phrase.en: At least I've still got the strength.
phrase.pinyin: hái hǎo wǒ hái yǒu lì qì

notes.body: The grand instruction to persist comes back to what remains in a body. 'At least' and 'still' make the claim finite: this is not a promise that effort will always be available or automatically rewarded. The ending finds something usable now. That scale gives the encouragement its force without turning the exhausted person into a failure for needing the quiet requested at the beginning.
notes.pinyinLabel: hái hǎo wǒ hái yǒu lì qì

tracks.intro: Never Give Up asks for quiet before it asks for endurance. The questions distinguish recognising a cruel situation from accepting it as the final shape of one's life. Perseverance then rests on a limited bodily fact: there is still some strength left. Unlike 'All In', the song does not make a particular rank or level of success the condition for stopping. Its encouragement is smaller and more credible because it acknowledges depletion rather than pretending that determination creates an inexhaustible person.

notes.title: Courteous threat

phrase.pinyin: qǐng nǐ xiān xiǎng qīng chǔ

notes.body: 请 supplies “please” to a warning surrounded by threats, so courtesy is doing coercive work. The later promise to stop being polite makes that tension explicit. The speaker presents himself as someone whose boundaries are reasonable and whose retaliation will be the other person’s responsibility. The civil phrasing is part of the threatening posture.
notes.pinyinLabel: qǐng nǐ xiān xiǎng qīng chǔ

notes.title: Blade eye

phrase.en: A sharp blade leaves its sheath.

notes.body: 利刃出鞘 is a compact, dramatic image of a weapon being drawn. Its four-character form and the impossible speed that follows give the threat a staged, cinematic sharpness. The target is specifically the eyes, preparing a song preoccupied with looking and reflection. The next admission of being deep in a role keeps that performance frame in view.

notes.title: Bone and backbone
notes.body: 骨气, literally “bone spirit,” means backbone or integrity: the ability to stand one’s ground. “Spineless” preserves a comparable bodily image. The insult follows the spectacular threat to another person’s eyes, making moral weakness physically legible. It is the vocabulary of a speaker measuring worth through firmness, even while insisting that others must stop judging him.

notes.title: Choice
notes.body: 选择权 does not just mean a preference; it is the right or power to choose. The sentence makes sovereignty over the self the core claim beneath the insults. Yet the planned red carpet and arriving reporters show that this self still anticipates an audience. The song seeks control over the terms of attention rather than total disappearance.

notes.title: An unpleasant smell
notes.body: 腥味 is the raw, fishy or bloody smell of flesh. 人多 makes it increase with the number of people, so a crowd becomes a bodily substance before it becomes company. Generic “stench” conveys disgust but loses that fleshy specificity. The line supplies a sensory rationale for withdrawal within this particularly hostile persona.

notes.title: Deep in the role
notes.body: He says he is deeply immersed in the role but not confused about it. That distinction puts the violent, vain persona on display as something performed with awareness. It also complicates the next claim that selfishness is his nature: the song alternates between costume and essence without settling which explains the other. Reading every threat or boast as a literal confession would miss the frame the lyric itself supplies.

notes.title: Keeping oneself good
notes.body: 独善其身 can praise maintaining one’s own integrity, but it can also criticize looking after only oneself. Both meanings are documented in the dictionary. “Selfish and conceited” soon follows, preventing a purely virtuous reading. The compact phrase lets self-preservation and self-absorption touch: keeping oneself intact may also mean withdrawing concern from everybody else.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 獨善其身

notes.title: Holding the gaze
notes.body: The early fantasy removes another person's eyes; the later gaze cannot turn away from the mirror. He rejects outside scrutiny while making his own looking the authority that declares him flawless. The prepared red carpet shows that he still wants to be seen, but on controlled terms. The issue is not simple invisibility. It is who is allowed to judge the image and what kind of judgement is permitted.

notes.title: Mirror flawless
notes.body: 无瑕 means without a blemish. The mirror produces complete satisfaction here, but “Sweet” later turns a demon-revealing mirror on the self to expose its true nature. Those two uses offer a useful contrast: reflection can flatter or uncover. The album does not give every mirror scene the same reassuring function.

notes.title: Red carpet

phrase.en: The red carpet's been laid out.
phrase.pinyin: hóng dì tǎn yǐ pū hǎo

notes.body: The scene moves from the private mirror to a prepared public entrance: carpet ready, reporters on the way. It makes the self-admiration part of a performance that is about to be seen. Hurry replaces contemplation. Even within the fantasy of complete control, somebody else’s arrival sets the timetable.
notes.pinyinLabel: hóng dì tǎn yǐ pū hǎo

notes.title: Good person

phrase.en: I can't be a good person anymore.
phrase.pinyin: bù néng zài dāng yí gè hǎo rén

notes.body: The claim that goodness has become impossible is justified by a private inventory of traps. That explanation makes the hardening understandable without making every subsequent act justified. The speaker can use injury both as a real memory and as permission to become less accountable. The song's acknowledgement of role-playing leaves that self-explanation open to inspection rather than presenting it as an unquestionable moral conclusion.
notes.pinyinLabel: bù néng zài dāng yí gè hǎo rén

notes.title: How much is enough?
notes.body: He calls his appetite small and still fears not getting enough. The admission interrupts flawless self-regard and a public scene of success with a much more basic insecurity. Being able to stage importance does not guarantee provision. The opponent's waste then becomes especially offensive because it appears beside a need the speaker presents as modest. The repeated threats return after this fear, making them sound defensive as well as triumphant.

notes.title: Denial ending

phrase.en: with cancer, but afraid to get treatment.
phrase.pinyin: dé le ái zhèng què bù gǎn zhì liáo

notes.body: The closing accusation pictures an extreme condition being left untreated while spending continues. It ends the contrast between the speaker’s fear of hunger and other people’s waste with an image of denial. The sharp turn from money to the body makes the accusation more than ordinary envy: resources are plentiful, but facing damage is continually deferred.
notes.pinyinLabel: dé le ái zhèng què bù gǎn zhì liáo

tracks.intro: Mirrors gives the speaker control over whose gaze counts. Other people's eyes are threatened, while his own reflection supplies flawless approval and prepares him for reporters. He calls this a role even as he names selfishness his true nature. The performance is therefore knowingly constructed, not a transparent record of uncomplicated self-love. A small appetite coupled with fear of hunger finally reveals the insecurity the grand image cannot remove. The return to the opening demands renews the defence rather than curing that fear.

notes.title: Knowing exactly how far to go
notes.body: 分寸 is the appropriate degree, boundary or tact a situation requires; 拿捏 means handling it with control. Together they boast of calibrated judgment, more specific than ordinary “balance.” The next lines give that judgment muscle memory and the authority of a veteran craftsperson. Skill is represented as something already embodied, requiring no visible hesitation.

notes.title: A practiced hand
notes.body: 老师傅 respectfully names an experienced craftsperson or skilled worker. It conveys competence acquired through practice rather than the mystical authority English “master” can suggest. Beside muscle memory and chess moves, it gives the opening a whole vocabulary of accumulated expertise. The later inability to find the way home makes that mastery deliberately incomplete.

notes.title: Chess

phrase.en: I've already made every move on the board.
phrase.pinyin: zǎo yǐ xià hǎo le měi yī bù qí

notes.body: Every move is supposedly already made, yet the next passage cannot answer where to go or fly. The contradiction distinguishes expertise from belonging. A person can be skilled at the activity through which they seek attention and still lack a place where the performance may stop. The opening reassurance is therefore also something the rest of the verse tests, rather than a neutral fact about the speaker's command of everything.
notes.pinyinLabel: zǎo yǐ xià hǎo le měi yī bù qí

notes.title: Flight pressure

phrase.en: After the big rises and falls, my ears always ring.
phrase.pinyin: dà qǐ dà luò hòu zǒng huì ěr míng

notes.body: 大起大落 conventionally means dramatic changes of fortune. Thoughts “flying” in the previous line make those rises and falls physical, and ringing ears give the figurative altitude a bodily aftereffect. The listener can hear career or emotional fluctuation and feel pressure at the same time. The lyric extends an idiom instead of simply naming it.
notes.pinyinLabel: dà qǐ dà luò hòu zǒng huì ěr míng

notes.title: A place out of the wind
notes.body: 避风塘 is a sheltered basin where boats can escape wind and rough weather. Coming after thoughts in flight and years of 闯荡, making one’s way through the world, it offers a place to stop without making stopping a defeat. The question that follows is not whether shelter would be welcome, but where such a place can actually be found.

notes.title: Home control

phrase.en: I can't find the way home.
phrase.pinyin: zhǎo bú dào huí jiā de lù

notes.body: The opening expert who has already made every chess move cannot solve the most ordinary navigation problem. That is the point of the reversal: being capable and confident does not guarantee a route back to safety. The next hoarse shout gives that lack a bodily cost, before he tries to answer it with yet more effort.
notes.pinyinLabel: zhǎo bú dào huí jiā de lù

notes.title: A body that cannot be written off
notes.body: Calling the self equipment that cannot yet be scrapped makes prior effort a claim on the present body. Rest risks making all that investment seem wasted. The next line answers lack of understanding with still more exertion, creating a loop in which failure of recognition demands further work. That is a harsher condition than ordinary ambition: usefulness becomes something the tired person has to keep proving.

notes.title: Effort with a life at stake
notes.body: 拼命 means exerting everything one has, literally staking life in the effort. The conjunction 所以, “so,” makes it the consequence of not being understood: recognition must be pursued through even more work. “Sweet” later says there is no need to 拼命. The phrase connects two conflicting ways of answering the same pressure, without requiring the tape to settle on one.

notes.title: Freedom mission
notes.body: The insistence on no mistakes and an important mission immediately precedes praise for an unrestrained life. The contradiction is local and specific. He may choose the work himself, but the standards governing it leave little room for error or rest. Freedom from other people's commands has not guaranteed freedom from command as a way of relating to oneself.

notes.title: Firm tofu
notes.body: Firm tofu is ordinary, pale and durable under cooking. It gives the claim to a clean conscience an unexpectedly modest body after all the expert and chess-master language. The fantasy is to remain recognisably oneself under prolonged pressure. The later admission of throwing a fit keeps that intactness from being purely serene: survival may preserve conviction without preserving the opening's perfect composure.

sources.label: Taishan College of Science and Technology: a tofu-making workshop

notes.title: His way of doing things
notes.body: 道 can be a road, a way of doing things or a guiding principle. The following challenge—how will you block it?—keeps the literal road alive inside the declaration. The line moves from having no route home to asserting a route of his own. That reversal makes the way both a direction of travel and a claim to live on his own terms.

notes.title: Throw fit
notes.body: 撒泼 means making an unruly, unreasonable scene to get one’s way. The speaker introduces it with 无奈之下, having no other option. That pairing presents loss of composure as a last available tactic. It undercuts the opening claim to perfectly measured judgment without erasing the conviction that he has a grievance worth pressing.

notes.title: An unsettled account
notes.body: 帐 is an account or ledger, and 没完 means it is not finished. A grievance becomes an unsettled balance still owed between two people. English “settling a score” uses a comparable transfer from accounting to conflict. The financial image also anticipates the later claim that others should have “bet” on him sooner: recognition and repayment keep borrowing the same vocabulary.

notes.title: A dangerous invitation
notes.body: At the Hongmen banquet in Sima Qian’s history, Fan Zeng arranges a sword dance as cover for killing Liu Bang during Xiang Yu’s feast. The name has become shorthand for hospitality hiding danger. The next lyric’s “acting skills” is especially apt: the historical threat was itself disguised as entertainment. Polite performance and hostile intention occupy the same room.

sources.label: Sima Qian: the Hongmen banquet in 項羽本紀

notes.title: Closed room
notes.body: 闲人勿扰 has the clipped tone of a sign on a door: people without business here should stay out. The next line shuts the room tight, while the speaker narrates what “they” are discussing inside. The sequence turns exclusion around. He may be outside their conversation, but the song lets him supply its embarrassing content.

notes.title: Betting on a person
notes.body: 押 is staking a bet. The imagined doubters do not merely regret failing to like him; they regret failing to back him while the outcome was uncertain. Their recognition arrives as a missed opportunity. The line turns exclusion into evidence of their poor judgment, letting the speaker narrate the private conversation he assumes they are now having.

notes.title: Recognition on whose terms?
notes.body: Freshness and classic status are normally judged on different timelines, but he offers the same immediate answer to both. The repeated 'right in front of you' refuses further delay. This returns to the opening effort to attract attention after a verse about its exhausting costs. The point is less that the speaker has objectively proved either category than that waiting for permission to count has become intolerable.

tracks.intro: Ume begins and ends by asking to be recognised, while its middle reveals the cost of trying to make recognition inevitable. The expert who has planned every move cannot find home; the supposedly free person is governed by deadlines and a ban on mistakes. Firm tofu offers a comic image of surviving pressure intact, but a later tantrum disrupts the claim to perfect judgement. The final demand is immediate: stop postponing your verdict about the fresh or the classic when the person asking is already here.

notes.title: Love of country as a ledger

phrase.en: Who dares say I don't love China
phrase.pinyin: shuí gǎn shuō wǒ bù ài zhōng guó

notes.body: The opening does not simply announce patriotism; it challenges somebody's right to deny it. Its evidence is unusually concrete: taxes, money spent at home, a free show and travel costs paid for others. Those are claims made by the lyric, not independently verified accounts. Their argumentative function is clear: the speaker wants material contributions judged instead of accepting a loyalty test defined entirely by someone else's interpretation of his image or associations.
notes.pinyinLabel: shuí gǎn shuō wǒ bù ài zhōng guó

notes.title: Tax drugs

phrase.en: I pay my taxes, don't do drugs,
phrase.pinyin: jiāo zhe shuì bù xī dú

notes.body: Two ordinary claims of lawful behavior become the opening evidence in a defense of patriotism. The verb form 交着 makes tax payment ongoing. Later 本人, “I personally,” gives a declaration about legality the tone of a formal statement. The speaker alternates bureaucratic respectability with profanity, using each register to mock the conditions under which he is being judged.
notes.pinyinLabel: jiāo zhe shuì bù xī dú

notes.title: Economic register

phrase.pinyin: cù jìn shè huì jīng jì fā zhǎn

notes.body: Ordinary spending becomes a contribution to social and economic development. The policy-report phrasing is both a joke about inflated language and a serious move within the argument: if these are the official-sounding terms of value, his conduct can be described in them too. Bureaucratic respectability and profanity are therefore not random stylistic opposites. They let him enter the judging vocabulary and then mock the people claiming exclusive authority to use it.
notes.pinyinLabel: cù jìn shè huì jīng jì fā zhǎn

notes.title: Own pocket

phrase.en: Put up 20,000 of my own money

notes.body: 自掏 emphasizes money coming from his own pocket. 免费 makes the event free for the audience, not costless to produce. That difference is the substance of his claim: a public benefit can depend on a private expense people do not see. The round figure makes the contribution sound materially countable rather than merely virtuous.

notes.title: Flights and hotels
notes.body: 机酒 compresses 机票, plane tickets, and 酒店, hotels, into two characters. 报 is the practical language of covering or reimbursing an expense. The phrase makes the defense unusually concrete: support for other people has receipts, travel arrangements and a bill. It also briefly brings a working performer’s logistics into the grander rhetoric about loving a country.

notes.title: An unresolved target
notes.body: 根茎 literally means a root and stem, but 摸着, fondling, makes the bodily and sexual insult hard to miss. The opponent is pictured as deriving authority from intimacy with a “music uncle,” rather than producing an independent idea. What the line clearly supplies is a vulgar image of deference under the following mock praise for a great intellectual leader.

phrase.pinyin: yīn yuè dà shū de gēn jīng

notes.pinyinLabel: yīn yuè dà shū de gēn jīng

notes.title: Scolding the scolders
notes.body: He crowns the opponent a great philosophical leader while reducing himself to a hip-hop fool, then asks why such a superior figure is attacking him. This is mock deference used to expose a mismatch between claimed stature and behaviour. The subsequent formal demand for decorum lets the supposedly uncultivated person deliver the lesson. No name is supplied, so the rhetorical relation is clearer than the identity of the target.

notes.title: Thunder without rain
notes.body: 雷声大雨点小 means a lot of thunder with little rain: impressive noise followed by little result. The next image makes that noisy agitation into little monkeys jumping around. The idiom strips the antagonists of the power their activity claims, preparing the speaker’s casually cruel invitation to keep getting angry.

phrase.en: lots of thunder and hardly any rain
phrase.pinyin: léi shēng dà yǔ diǎn xiǎo

notes.pinyinLabel: léi shēng dà yǔ diǎn xiǎo

notes.title: Zoo gates

phrase.pinyin: dòng wù yuán de dà mén

notes.body: After calling his antagonists monkeys, he says they have never left the zoo. The enclosure extends the animal insult into a claim about limited experience: loud judgment comes from inside a bounded world. Against his earlier movement between foreign earnings and domestic spending, the image makes range of experience another contested source of authority.
notes.pinyinLabel: dòng wù yuán de dà mén

notes.title: A taunt disguised as encouragement

phrase.en: Make sure you try harder in your next life
phrase.pinyin: xià bèi zi yí dìng yào nǔ lì a

notes.body: The grammar sounds encouraging—“make sure you work hard”—but the next chance has been postponed until another lifetime. That is the insult. It follows “die mad” and leads into the affectionate “little darlings,” so supportive phrasing is repeatedly used to belittle. The encouragement works by imposing a very long wait.
notes.pinyinLabel: xià bèi zi yí dìng yào nǔ lì a

notes.title: Anger cutesy

phrase.pinyin: zì bēi de bǎo bèi men

notes.body: 宝贝们 is affectionate and plural, but 自卑 assigns the recipients insecurity. The phrase performs tenderness while claiming the authority to explain their anger for them. It belongs with “try harder next life”: the antagonism repeatedly arrives dressed as care. English needs the surrounding taunts to keep “darlings” from sounding genuinely consoling.
notes.pinyinLabel: zì bēi de bǎo bèi men

notes.title: Influence recast as missionary work
notes.body: 传教 literally means spreading a religion. Applied to the rivals’ cultural taste, it makes them followers of a doctrine handed down by somebody else. 糟粕 is the dregs or discarded residue, so even that received wisdom is downgraded. The accusation is sharper than ordinary copying: they claim authority while treating another person’s leftovers as revelation.

notes.title: His own complaint about overreading

phrase.en: reading a bit too much into it

notes.body: 想得有点多 is a conversational way of saying somebody is reading too much into things or imagining implications that are not there. 有点, “a bit,” gives the accusation a superficially mild form after several much harsher insults. The address still remains personal. The song resists being told what it must stand for by reducing the opponent’s theory to overthinking.

notes.title: Faces and hidden knives
notes.body: 两面三刀 is a fixed expression for duplicity—different faces in different company, with harm concealed beneath them. It works through an accumulation of surfaces and weapons rather than literally counting knives. Calling that figure a spy intensifies the mistrust: bad faith becomes the role of someone secretly serving another interest.

notes.title: A nationally charged insult
notes.body: The charged accusation of betrayal is turned back on an opponent in an exaggerated comparison. This complicates the opening defence: the speaker refuses someone else's loyalty judgement while enjoying the same vocabulary as an offensive weapon. The final appeal to common roots does not cancel that escalation. The song is compelling partly because solidarity and retaliatory exclusion remain entangled inside its own speech.

sources.label: jackzebra: official discography, 王中王 track 34

notes.title: Inspiration conversion

phrase.pinyin: quán bù dōu shì wǒ de líng gǎn

notes.body: The antagonists stop being only people who judge him and become material he can select and use. That reverses the direction of control. Their attempts to define his work now contribute to the work, and the pocketed-creature image gives the conversion a comic physical form. It is a creative response to the dispute, although not complete indifference: the amount of attention spent on them shows that their judgement still has force.
notes.pinyinLabel: quán bù dōu shì wǒ de líng gǎn

notes.title: A possible Pocket Monsters wink

phrase.en: stuff them all in my pocket

notes.body: The paired 精灵, little creatures, and 口袋, pocket, evoke Pokémon’s Pocket Monsters name and its Chinese “pocket creatures” associations. The word pairing gives the preceding insults a playful second scene. Each strange antagonist can be pocketed as another piece of material for a song: collecting irritations becomes a way to turn them into something useful.

notes.title: One ear
notes.original: 一只耳朵进一只耳朵出

phrase.zh: 一只耳朵进一只耳朵出
phrase.en: In one ear and out the other
phrase.pinyin: yī zhī ěr duǒ jìn yī zhī ěr duǒ chū

notes.body: The same idiom works naturally in English: words pass through without being retained. Here it follows the accusation that someone cannot distinguish kind speech from abuse and leads into an instruction to read more. Hearing, interpreting and learning are separated into three failures. The demand for better judgment is expressed through a deliberately elementary lesson.
notes.pinyinLabel: yī zhī ěr duǒ jìn yī zhī ěr duǒ chū

notes.title: The elevated family of China
notes.body: 华夏 is a literary-cultural name for China; 儿女 casts belonging as membership in one family. That elevated kinship language is immediately followed by calling someone stupid as a pig. The collision is the point. Solidarity does not magically erase the anger, and the final same-root poem must speak across insults the song itself is still delivering.

notes.title: Born from one root
notes.body: The familiar poem's beans are destroyed by fire made from their own stems. Shared origin is turned into the means of injury. After 'children of China', the quotation asks why belonging should organise attacks among people it could instead connect. But the preceding pig insult remains part of the appeal. The ending reaches for solidarity from inside an angry exchange, making the wish meaningful without pretending the speaker has already escaped the conflict.

phrase.en: We were born from the same root

tracks.intro: Inspiration disputes who gets to judge the speaker's belonging and what evidence should count. Taxes, domestic spending and paid travel become an answer to accusations of disloyalty; inflated civic language and crude insults make that answer combative and funny. The opponents are then converted into creative material, changing their attack into something the song can use. The final same-root appeal widens belonging beyond the speaker, but it does not erase his taunts. The track both resists and reproduces the rhetoric of loyalty it is fighting over.

notes.title: Right paths

phrase.en: Every path was the right one.
phrase.pinyin: suǒ yǒu de lù dōu shì duì de

notes.body: 所有, every, leaves no wrong turn outside the opening verdict. Yet the song that follows is full of exhaustion, disappointment and self-questioning. The confidence therefore sounds retrospective: a route can have been worth taking without every moment on it having felt right. The closer begins with affirmation, then refuses to tidy up what that affirmation cost.
notes.pinyinLabel: suǒ yǒu de lù dōu shì duì de

notes.title: Own eye
notes.body: 眼光 is judgment, discernment or taste as well as an eye’s reach. The self-congratulation plants the visual vocabulary that will become magnifying glass, telescope and mirror. At first he praises his ability to choose; later the useful vision is the ability to see himself. The track gradually turns outward-looking taste toward self-recognition.

notes.title: Taking notes on ordinary life
notes.body: A trainee reporter is a modest identity for someone who later claims the number-one place. It makes music a way of noticing and recording the surrounding world before it is a hierarchy to win. That fits the album's accumulation of daily objects, quoted speech and grotesque social scenes. Yet the reporter soon says he knows everything already. The tension between observation and exhausted certainty is present from the start.

notes.title: The same word for formulas and scams
notes.body: 套路 can be an established sequence, a formula or a manipulative routine. The next line’s repeated melodies brings the word directly into music, while “Ghost Dog” used it for distrusted social behavior. The recurrence connects two frustrations without making them identical: a predictable song and a predictable interaction can both feel as though the outcome has been arranged in advance.

notes.title: An easy ascent that still leaves wealth distant
notes.body: Immediately after rejecting shortcuts and reaching the summit in one step, the lyric puts people inside an elevator looking toward distant wealth. They have a mechanical route upward, yet the desired destination remains far away. The sigh punctures the fantasy of easy ascent. Movement and attainment are separated in a few ordinary objects.

notes.title: Wealth mountains
notes.body: Gold and silver become entire mountains, giving wealth a size that overwhelms the people inside the elevator. The preceding 登顶, reaching a summit, makes the mountains both treasure and destination. This is aspiration rendered as landscape: something visible in the distance can structure a life’s motion while remaining out of reach.

notes.title: A mirror that exposes monsters
notes.body: The revealing mirror is turned on the self, while the magnifying glass and telescope are declared less useful. The comparison changes the purpose of seeing: collecting more detail or reaching farther does not replace recognising one's own nature. Unlike the flawless reflection in 'Mirrors', this instrument is valuable because it can expose what a pleasing appearance conceals. The real blessing is not perfect innocence but a less flattering kind of access to oneself.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 照妖鏡

notes.title: Blessing
notes.body: 福气 names good fortune or the benefit of being blessed. The “real” version here is not first place or the gold-and-silver mountains: it is being able to recognize his own nature. “Mirrors” had good fortune shining beside a flawless reflection. The changed emphasis keeps the album’s language of blessing active while revising what counts as a fortunate outcome.

notes.title: Machine
notes.body: 台 is the classifier for a machine, and 一台 makes the whole world one piece of equipment. The next complaint is that being himself is difficult because so many things affect him. The image supplies pressure and interdependence without explaining a complete system. It lets the lyric register being acted on before turning to the private war he fights inside that world.

notes.title: Private war
notes.body: 自己的 locates the conflict with the speaker, even though the previous lines describe forces acting on him from outside. The battle is not given a named enemy or a decisive victory. Its consequence is ongoing wear on mind and soul, followed by the unsettling claim to love the pain. The verse asks what sustained struggle does to the person who makes it habitual.

notes.title: Time boils the rain
notes.body: 时间煮雨 is also the title of Yisa Yu’s 2013 song for the film Tiny Times. The exact phrase supplies a recognizable Mandopop echo here. Grammatically it makes time perform an impossible kitchen action, boiling rain, inside a reflection on two years of experience. The wording borrows an atmosphere of time passing without needing to reproduce or retell the other song.

sources.label: Yisa Yu: 时间煮雨, Tiny Times film song

notes.title: First place

phrase.pinyin: zhè dì yī shì wǒ de

notes.body: The claim arrives immediately after wanting the torment to end. He is not simply announcing retirement from competition; the desire to win interrupts the wish to stop. This is central to the closer's honesty. The pressure is not only imposed by outsiders, because the speaker also wants the distinction the contest promises. Later advice to treat it as play has to contend with that investment rather than merely dismiss other people's demands.
notes.pinyinLabel: zhè dì yī shì wǒ de

notes.title: Rollercoaster

phrase.en: A roller coaster without an end
phrase.pinyin: méi yǒu jìn tóu de guò shān chē

notes.body: A roller coaster promises controlled ups and downs followed by an exit. Removing the end leaves the sensation without the reassurance that it is temporary. The preceding pairs move from anticipation to loss, excitement to numbness; the ride turns those emotional changes into a track laid out in advance. Repetition becomes tiring even when the peaks are real.
notes.pinyinLabel: méi yǒu jìn tóu de guò shān chē

notes.title: A life reduced to a swipe

phrase.en: One swipe of a thumb and it's gone
phrase.pinyin: dà mǔ zhǐ yī huà ér guò

notes.body: The roller coaster gives the maker a long, exhausting sequence of expectation and disappointment. A single thumb movement then traverses it from the viewer's side. The unequal duration is the injury: what takes over one person's life can occupy only an instant of another's attention. The line helps explain why recognition never seems adequate to the effort spent pursuing it, without accusing every individual listener of deliberate cruelty.
notes.pinyinLabel: dà mǔ zhǐ yī huà ér guò

notes.title: Playing after insisting on first place
notes.body: The instruction to keep it playful echoes a recurring concern in Jackzebra’s catalog: his 2024 弓长张 EP includes 认真你就输了, whose title says taking it seriously means losing. Here the advice clashes with the refusal to surrender first place just earlier. Play is both a creative freedom and a defense against how much the contest already matters.

sources.label: jackzebra: official discography, 弓长张 EP

notes.title: No self sacrifice

phrase.en: No need to give your life to it.

notes.body: The key claim is that total exertion is not necessary. 'Ume' made that same life-staking effort the inevitable answer to being misunderstood; here the speaker withdraws the obligation. He can still care about music or rank while questioning whether either deserves the whole person. The force of the advice comes from the unresolved competitive refrain nearby: this is a limit being argued for from inside the attachment.

notes.title: Immortal as a laughingstock
notes.body: 名垂青史 usually celebrates a name preserved in history. Adding 笑柄, a laughingstock, reverses the honor: lasting remembrance becomes lasting ridicule. This answers “Morning,” where dissolving into the river of history meant nobody would remember him. Across the two songs, being forgotten and being remembered wrongly become rival fears.

notes.title: Answering an older title
notes.body: The line reverses Zhang Chu's song title about lonely people being shameful, then eventually promotes them from not shameful to great. Repetition first removes a stigma and then supplies a counter-claim to worth. But the song continues into muttering, audience pressure and disappointment. The defence is a valuable position reached within the closer, not a magical resolution of its social isolation. Its insistence records how much defending is still needed.

sources.label: Zhang Chu: 孤独的人是可耻的

notes.title: Talking to himself, then out of words
notes.body: 无语 commonly expresses exasperation, disbelief or having no adequate response, not literal loss of speech. It shares 语, “speech,” with the preceding 自语, talking to oneself. The paired words let him keep narrating while claiming to be beyond words. The song stages that contradiction rather than hiding it: speechlessness itself becomes another line to say.

notes.title: What recognition adds

phrase.pinyin: guān zhòng men de qī pàn

notes.body: The audience's word is expectant hope, not an explicit threat. The next line names what that hope becomes for the performer: pressure that may be invisible to the people generating it. This broadens the album's earlier hostile-audience scenes. Even sympathetic attention can become a demand when somebody must repeatedly supply the version of themselves that others are waiting for. The burden does not require every listener to be an enemy.
notes.pinyinLabel: guān zhòng men de qī pàn

notes.title: From knowing everything to trusting ignorance
notes.body: The final refuge contradicts both the opening claim to know everything and the earlier celebration of self-recognition. That contradiction should remain. The speaker has seen enough to want relief from seeing, yet cannot simply unlearn the experience the song has narrated. Repeating absolute belief in ignorance creates a wished-for shelter in language. The album ends with that effort to stop being burdened by knowledge, rather than a proof that the burden has gone.

notes.title: Belief ending
notes.body: 深信不疑 is a firm idiom for profound, unquestioning belief. Its object is the claim that ignorance brings happiness, so the song ends with certainty about the value of not knowing. After self-examination and awareness of treacherous hearts, that conviction sounds like a refuge constructed in language. The repeated affirmation does not erase everything he has just shown us he knows.

tracks.intro: Sweet closes the mixtape by arguing with the drives that have kept it moving. The speaker values self-recognition over distant wealth, wants the struggle to end and immediately refuses to surrender first place. Attention compresses a life of effort into a thumb swipe; play is offered as protection against giving that contest everything. The defence of lonely people is emphatic but not the final resolution. Audience expectations and a wish for ignorance follow. The closer finds moments of self-acceptance without claiming that insight has removed the pressure to perform.

researchContext.title: The record
researchContext.body: Zhuang Zhuang Mixtape arrived on Surf Gang on October 2, 2026: 55 tracks, opening with Sour and closing with Sweet. Its cast widens from YoungQueenz on Poker Face to User116, Effie, kuru, yoyi, 春 and 南部犯罪份子. Aghast has a production credit on every track from Hitman through Snatch, giving that stretch a shared collaborator behind its changing scenes.

researchContext.title: How the words take shape
researchContext.body: Jackzebra told AVYSS that he writes while singing over a beat he has listened to repeatedly, keeping the images in his head central. He values the room Mandarin leaves for indirect meanings. Listen for ordinary phrases becoming physical scenes: familiarity becomes cooking, authority becomes family seniority, and a tired saying suddenly turns into a threat.

researchContext.title: A mixtape made with friends
researchContext.body: In STATIC, he describes mixtapes as a format for letting ideas flow, reserving an official debut album for later. In a separate conversation about Above & Beyond, he compared that earlier tape to a collection of his producer friends’ work. The credits here likewise reward attention: long-running collaborators sit alongside guests working in Mandarin, Korean and English.

researchContext.title: Everyday details
researchContext.body: The small details connect to his stated interests: he has described playing Temple Run in transit and before shows, watching Top Boy, and wanting to score White Oleander. These give the songs specific points of contact with his life. The notes follow those connections alongside the lyrics’ jokes, invented scenes and competing voices.

researchContext.title: Reading closely
researchContext.body: Jackzebra has pushed back on being made to represent all of China’s underground. These notes stay close to the words: what an expression usually means, what changes in this line, and how another song answers it. Cultural references have sources; interpretations rest on details you can hear or read in the song.
